FIER GARDEN.

What years 11;;;;liPPe-d-sin-ce those last hours We tarried in this garden-plot; Amid her sweet, old-fashioned flow'rs, Pansies and pinks and bergamot. The peonies were full of bloom, Lupins and lilies 'mid their green; And dahlias, that through the gloom Glimmered and shone like stars terrenne. Her roses, too—by many a sage In rose-lore reckoned worth renown—

- Of varied tint, in varied stage, Here bud, here bloom, here dropping down. Again, in tender fancy's freak, I seem to learn their names from her, The "Damask," "Blush," and this antique Twi-coloured "York and Lancaster." I see her deft hands cull and store— Vlihere'er decay perfection mars— The fragrant, falling petals for Her bowls and tall pot-pourri jars. Vain thought! A wild, untended air Lies over path and flow'r and tree; They lack the impress of her care, Th' influence of her ministry. Unheeded now the roses blow, And strew their loveliness around; Untrained, the clematis trails low, And weeds make waste the pleasant ground. Moss-grown the paths are, and a-fringe With unkempt grasses either side; The little sate creaks on its hinge, Now rocking to, now opening wide. As if to ape a joyance gone. Some birds a sudden treble raise; While still the little gate creaks on, And lets in careless waifs and strays. A haunted place; whose shadows fall Over my spirit, sad and deep; Since the loved hands that tended all Were clasped so long ago in sleep. .--The Magazine of Art. KATE CARTER.

div.head: Varittito.
div.p: Varittito.

Truth, like the sunbeam, cannot be soiled by any • outward touch. Purposes, like eggs, unless they be hatched into action, will run into decay. Old Mrs.liently (in an art gallery) : "The programme saysthat's the Venus of Milo." Old Mr. Bently : " I reckon she must have been killed in a railroad accident, 2dirandy." Kindly feeling begets kindly feeling; happiness cannot exist and exert its influence without conveying happiness to those around. We are all in search of the one great ideal, universal lasting happiness; therefore we should all join in doing our best to push on the much-desired end, and in the meantime be content with the best that we can get. The following are extracts from the American negro's philosophy :—Dar's only a mighty short step 'twixt seifishness'ari' dishonesty. It is strong selfishness dat makes a man steal.—De man wid a thinkin' mind is never alone 'cept when he's in company, an' is neber in company 'cept when he's alone.—Too much 'potence ken be laid ter de openness of de eye. De owl has got a heap bigger eye dan de fox, but he am n got half as much sense.—When a man wanster to prube eberything what he say, I's sorter 'specious, hut when he wanster bet on eberything he says, I know dal- he's a liar.—lmitation is sometimes prized higher dan de 'riginal. De mockin' bird dat caws like do crow is more 'spected dan de crow, but he suffers on die account, fur de white folks put him in a cage. It is a pity dat all imatators ain't shut THOUGHTS re OUR ORCIIARD.—Nova the ripened boughs are "big with bending fruit," the apples glow like fire between the leaves, the pears drop down upon the grass, the plums make a rich show on many a sun-kissed wall. Go shares," says a pastor, "is an excellent rule to do with everything we get, not only as children." There have been seasons when fruit-growers declared it scarcely paid them to pick the fruit, there was so much of it; but London Sunday School teachers and other workers, arranging festivals with scanty funds, could have told of eager eyes and ready lips still more plentiful. and of workrooms. sick chambers, lonely ones to whom a gift of fruit would have seemed a God-send. In sending flowers to the city, let us bear in mind just now a guer- don of fruit likewise. And as we stand among these trees that have fulfilled the promise of their blossom, should we not humbly ask ourselves if He who has spared us year by year is finding fruit to His praise? There are many whose bloom the world has beheld, of whom He may be sighing now, "Nothing but leaves ; " there are those to whom earth scarce gives a thought, who are bringing forth fruit an hundredfold beneath the sunshine of the Master's smiles. One of Mrs. Presser's helpful little fables concerns an espalier loaded with fruit, reproached by a tall apple-tree because its branches were lying on the ground. -"Every one admires my fruit," it said: "no one can see whether you've any fruit or not..."—" I'm not too low down," said the espalier, " for the master to find it when the time comes ;till then I am content to wait." —The Quiver. As; AMERICAN "DAISY."—Won't this American daisy compare favourably with the shamrock? A short time ago, in a village not so very far from the city of Roches- ter, a political aspirant for office with an oleaginous tongue was stumping for the support of the farmers at the impending election. Discovering, to his dismay, after half an hour's liberal expenditure of perspiration and logie,that he was exciting no interest, lie determined to conquer his audience by flattery, and this he proceeded to do somewhat in this style I have always had a leaning toward farmers. I admire and love them, and for their vocation I entertain the most profound respect. It is the noblest and most honourable of occupations. All the virtues grow spontaneously on a farm. Every man should be a tiller of the soil, and every woman a dairymaid. I married a farmer's daughter. I popped to her at four o'clock in the morning, when she was milking. I can never forget the incident, for in her con- fusion she lost her grip of an Alderney's teat and shot a stream of milk into my eye. She was the cream of her sex, gentlemen. Yes, the country's the place to be born in, and to live in, and I speak from personal experience, for my cradle was the gentle swaying bough, and my lullaby the gurgling of the brook and the songs of birds. Yes, I know all about a farm." And here stretching himself to his full height, and drawing a long breath, he shouted (and this "blast upon his bug,lehorn was worth" —he thought—" a thousand men") : "Why, my friends, I was raised in a cornfield !" A declaration that elicited from an inspired husbandman the cry: "Pumpkin, be gosh r'—c. G., in Harper's Monthly. THE GATHERING 05 THE CLANS.—This "gathering of the clans" goes back to a remote antiquity, tradition assigning it to the days of Malcolm Canmore. It is said to have thus originated :—Having a mind to establish a sort of post system by means of foot-runners, Malcolm summoned his subjects to meet him at the place where now stands the Castle of Braemar. When they were assembled, a purse of gold, with a full suit of dress and arms, were offered to the man who first reached the sum- mit of Craig Chionaisith, i.e„ Kenneth's Craig, as seen from the place where the king and people were assem- bled." The competitors were placed, the signal for starting given, and tne runners bounded across the plain. They had almost reached the foot of the hill when another competitor, the youngest son of Macgregor of Ballochbhui hastened to the king, and pleaded for leave to run also. Malcolm told him it was hopeless for him to win, but allowed him to start. He rapidly gained upon the runners, among whom were his two eldest brothers. Up the steep, rugged slope he went, and now had passed all except his own brothers, who were the fore- most. He now drew level with the second. • Halves, brother,' he cried, and I'll stop r 'Gain what you can, and keep what you get; I'll do the same,' was the answer of one; while the other was too breathless to speak." Be was now level with the foremost—again made the same offer, and received the same answer. "Now they were in sight of the goal, but every muscle and nerve was already tightened to breaking. Terribly pressed was the elder brother • but, determined to gain, he put out his hand to impede the progrees of the younger. Feeling nothing, he looked round, expecting to seo his brother on the ground, while at that moment the youngest leaped forward below the outstretched arm. Furious, the eldest brother bounded on after him, and fell just as his hand clutched with maddened grasp the kilt of his rivaL Encouraged by the accident, those in the rear came pressing forward, when, quick as thought, the youngest Macgregor unbuckled his kilt, saying, as he did so, 'I have yielded all to you hitherto; take that also.' Then, springing forward, he seized the signal- staff, and, throwing it up in the air, sank down on the earth beside it."—Our Own Country. div.head: THE.FREE LIBRARY MOVEMENT IN
div.p: THE.FREE LIBRARY MOVEMENT IN

WARRINGTON. On Monday evening a meeting of persons inter- ested in the movement for freeing the Warrington Public Library was held at the Horsemarket-street Cocoa Rooms. Although the meeting had been pri- vately convened on short notice, the large meeting room was crowded by those who were ,present. Amongst those in attendance were the Revs. S. Wilkinson, J. Yonge, J. J. Langham, and G. Allton, Dr. Oornall, J.P. ; Councillors W. Pierpoint, F. A. Roberts. and Dixon; Messrs F. Monks, J.P., T. Mor- ris, J. Walker, H. Whitham, T. Flood, J. Grifiths,R. Roberts, W. Roberts, &c. Mr. Morris was elected to preside. The CHAIRMAN said they had now been working in that movement for freeing the library about two years, and he could hardly say how much nearer the end they were. There were some of hisfriends in that room who had waited upon the monied men of the town and county within three or four miles radius.but they had fared somewhat badly. although they had got some promises. They knew that the sub-committee appointed by the Jubilee demon- stration committee had met a deputation of the Library Committee at Mr. Robert Davies's office, and gone into the matter with them, but at a sub- sequent meeting of the Library Committee the whole thing was again brushed to one side. He must say that he felt disgusted, but still, while dis- gusted, he never lost heart, and he hoped that they would yet overcome that—what might he call it? —nasty indisposition to help the working-man to the book which he truly paid for, as truly as he paid for the bread lie ate. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.) , Mr. T. FLOOD then gave an account of the inter- views which he and other members of the deputa- tion appointed by the working-men's committee had had with some leading local gentlemen'. They ' had waited, he said, upon Mr. Glazebrook Rylands, who gave them to understand that if he could do anything to promote the interests of working-men 1 in connection with the library be would do so, but at the same time he did not seem desirous of pledging himself in any way. He, however, pro- mised that he would be willing to give them some pecuniary aid, provided the thing was put into shape. The next gentleman they saw was Mr. John Crosfield, whose large heartedness in connection , with educational matters they all knew. Mr. Cros- field seemed to be imbued with one or two ideas against their scheme, but with the assistance of ' Mr. Whitham they very soon disabused his mind of them. In the end Mr. Crosfield said he was pre- pared to go as far as anybody else in the matter, but he was not prepared to pledge himself as to what he would really give. On another occasion they had an interview with Sir Gilbert Greenall, and told him of their success with the other two gentlemen. Sir Gilbert replied that what others did he would do, and beyond that they did not get. (Hear, hear.) Mr. H. WHITHAM said that Mr. Crosfield had told them that if it were a mere question of ways and means, that should not stand in the way of the free- ing of the library. He was of opinion that if the Town Council once accepted the principle that it was desirable to have a free lending library the money ought to be forthcoming from one source or another, and he for one would do what he could to help. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Whitham then referred to the fact that Councillor F. A. Roberts had asked a question at the last Council meeting as to the legality of the present mode of conducting the library. The answer of Alderman Webster to that question was, he considered, anything but satisfac- tory as it could be twisted into almost any shape. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Whitham also urged that the committee for conducting the movement should he made as influential as possible, and concluded by saying that no member of the Town Council, whether Liberal or Tory, should have his vote un- less he pledged himself to the free library move- ment. (Applause.) Mr. JOHN WALKER said he did not think they could do anything more than what had been done in the direction of endeavouring to persuade people to advance money. They must now, he thought, seek to convince their rulers by putting pressure upon them. (Hear, hear.) His suggestion would be that, as they did not seem to be able to move the Museum and Library Committee in the matter of ways and means, they should play what to him had always seemed their trump card, and fall back upon their constitutional right to have a free lending library. (Applause.) As had been already stated, Id. in the pound was taken from every ratepayer in the borough for the purposes of the library, while the Act by which these libraries were instituted made no provision whatever outside the id. in the pound for subscribers to receive privileges. His contention was, and he had even had legal opinion, that the Library Committee were acting utterly illegally in taking these subscriptions and giving *special privileges for them. They were not wrong in receiving subscriptions, but in giving privileges to one ratepayer over another, which the law did not permit. (Hear, hear.) He knew that one member of the Library Committee admitted that he thought the course taken by the committee was one that could not be justified by the law. He would suggest that they pass a resolution asking the Mayor to call at once a public meeting on that question purely and simply. He would suggest that this meeting be held before the next Council .meeting, and if the Council did not take some steps in the matter satisfactory to the ratepayers, then he should urge that they organise to fight every ward in the town, if the member for each ward would not pledge himself on that quastion. (Ap- plause.) Mr. F. MONKS thought the scheme would not be furthered by people saying what they would do in this case or the other. He knew that considerable difficulty had been created by the threats already used. If it be the wish of the town that the library should be free, there was no power in Warrington that could prevent it from being free. It was a matter that rested to a very large extent with the Corporation, because the Corporation had the appointment of the committee which had the management of the library. That being so, it was a question that could be settled in the Town Council without doing any harm. He himself had very great respect for Mr. Beall-lent, and would be very sorry to act in any way to cause him annoyance. He believed that Mr. Beamont was as anxious to do what he considered to be best in tbe interest of the town as Mr. Walker or Mr. Morris, but lie did not see in the way that they did. He was quite aware that considerable mischief had been done in the past by the Library Committee itself, for the very valuable library of Mr. John Robson had been lost to the town entirely through a misunderstanding. (Hear, hear.) if misunder- standings like this could be avoided in the present case it would be better. (Hear, hear.) He found that workpeople could spend money freely on other things, but were unwilling to spend 5s a year in subscribing to the library. He mentioned this be- cause he knew it was an idea that ran through a good many minds. (A Voice: "The workpeople pay for the library already," and hear, hear.) He happened to know what was the opinion of three or four influential members of the Library Commit- tee, and he knew that they had no objection to the principle Of a free lending library. div.head: BOWLING AI &TM FS. _ BOWLING AT ARPLEY.
div.p: BOWLING AI &TM FS. _ BOWLING AT ARPLEY.

A main of bowls took place on the ground of the Arpley Cricket and Bowling Club on Saturday after- noon, and, although the entries were not so numer- ous as had been anticipted, the game was keenly contested throughout. The five prizes offered were awarded as follows :-1, Mr. W. Dooley; 2, Mr. Hugh Ferguson; 3, Mr. Greenwood; 4, Mr. Cortin; 5, Mr. Jlames Bolton.

div.head: BANK QUAY BOWLING GREEN.
div.p: BANK QUAY BOWLING GREEN.

On Saturday afternoon, a well-contested open main of bowls took place on the Bank Quay Sub- scription Bowling Club green, a large number of spectators being present. The green was in capital condition. thanks to the attention bestowed upon it by Mr. Mellor, of the Bowling Green Inn. Thirty- two competitors took part, and the game resulted in a victory for Mr. William Gleave, Mr. William Massey being a good second, Mr. John Leigh third, and Mr. It. Brewster fourth. Four other players received minor prizes. MATCH. FOR .£25 _

On Saturday afternoon an interesting game was played on the green attached to the Bull's Head Inn. Church-street, between J. Shaw and J. Aridge, both local men, for £9...5 a-side. There was a fair attendance of spectators. The game was 101 up. Shaw, who has shown good form of late, was made a warm favourite, odds of 2 to 1 being laid on him shortly after the commencement of the game. The play was very good on the part of both, but even- tually Shaw proved his superiority. Bridge reached 11 to 8, when Shaw made a fine ran and went to 21 against 12. He subsequently totalled 32 to 16, 42 to ;.8, and 52 to 35, when there was a short inthrval. On resuming Bridge succeeded in re- ducing his leeway, but Shaw held the lead to the finish, winning by seven points. Totals—Shaw 101, Bridge 94. CONSERVATIVE CLUB BOWLING MAIN. _ _ . _

The annual main of bowls in connection with this club took place on Saturday. The managing com- mittee was composed of Messrs. John Roberts (chairman), Thomas Mason (hon. secretary), It. Isherwood, W. Watson, W.Whittaker, R. Chadwick, J. Leatherbarrow, J. Thornton' E. Green, A. Jolley, and. F. Turner, Councillor It. W. Francomb, Coun- cillor J. E. Wright, Mr. James Smethurst, and others were also present. The competitors numbered 52, and eight valuable prizes, subscribed for by various gentlemen, were competed for. Mr. John Roberts presented the prizes, but before doing so he thanked them for the honour thus conferred upon him, and added that he had been deputed by the committee to wait on Captain Reynolds and ask him if he would kindly pre- sent the prizes. That gentleman, however, declined, having resigned the chairmanship of the Association. They were all very sorry that he had been compelled through illhealth to resign, but he felt certain that Captain Reynolds would at all times give them his valuable advice and assistance. He was pleased to say that the green was in better order that day than it had been during the season, and he felt sure it was the wish of the Committee to do all they possibly could to make it perfect in every respect. They hoped before next season came to have it in such a condition that it would be a pleasure to those who played on it, and a source of satisfaction to the Committee. (Applause.) Mr. Roberts then presented the prizes as follows :-1, valuable timepiece, Thomas Cooper; 2, timepiece, W. Watson; 3, bowls and jack in case, G. IL Pick- stone; 4, bowls and jack, Frank Turner; 5, knives and forks (6), W. Potter; 6, copper kettle, G. Ogden; 7. umbrella, John Thornton; S. pipe and case, John llelsby.—Councillor It. W. Francomb proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman and Committee for the attention and trouble that they had given dur- ing the season. The workingmen after their day's word (he added) spent a pleasant hour in having a game at bowls, and he was sure they would benefit by such healthy exercise. (Applause.)--Councillor J. E. Wright seconded the proposition, and said he felt sure that every credit was due to the Commit- tee for the able manner in which the main had been got up and carried out. ( Ipplause.)—The vote of thanks was passed with applause.

Poor physical condition is largely answerable for a melancholy disposition, while high and bounding health prepares the way for bright hope and a glad outlook. To live then in a wholesome, sanitary manner, to observe in eating and drinking, in sleeping and waking, in woyk and amusement, the laws of physical well-being, rather than the mere indulgence of physical sensations, is a primary necessity for those who would preserve or attain a cheerful spirit,

He was right, for in another moment the men turned sharply to the left, and presently disappeared from view.

_ Lorraine looked at Ms watch. "In a quarter of an hour," he said, "they will be here, Hyacinth V'—He was holding a long American rifle u he spoke—one of those long-range weapons that a Western ranchmau regards with fatherly affection. The girl turned to him. "If your cousin, Tracy Mansfield," Lorraine went on, "comes on the scene, it will not be, I am afraid, as a peace-maker." "Vincent!"

Lorraine laid down the rifle, and took her hand. "Jealousy turns better men than he is into fiends, sweetheart; and I think Mansfield is capable of more evil than you deem. Very likely he will not believe that von came here of your own accord, but that I brought you; and then he will have good reason to urge the men to the uttermost; and if he believes that you came here, he will know that, after all, you do love me—perhaps think that you deceived him, and he would call that a bullet well sped that gave me my death." "lie spoke to you about me—at the ball," said Hyacinth: "Ho told you that!" "Yes." _ _

-"I did not conoiliate him, Hyacinth; my humour, I am afraid, hardly runs that way. Now for stern duty." He took up his position at the loophole, and Hya- cinth, standing near, Gould see if any form or head appeared. He knew she would not start or exclaim at anything, and so be could allow her to be close to him. " Hist! he whispered. suddenly, "I heard a voice." The rifle was shouldered in a second. Hyacinth held her breath. The sext second the forms of two men became visible. Not a leo% emetit from the girl, but her cheek went white. There was a sharp click—a loud report—an agonised cry, and Lorraine had sprung asidl, catching. Hyacinth's hand, and so drawing her quickly aside too. "I think that shot told," he said. " Sweetheart!" putting his arm about her, "why should you see such things?" "Why should I not ? my hand need not be idle." "You must be in no danger, Hyacinth," Lorraine said firmly. "I will do what you tell me—l will be an obedient lieutenant." He kissed ber_brow, and smiled," Come, then, to the oak room." A startled, bewildered pause had followed the 'first and fatal shot fired from the castle. The aim had been only too true. Dennis Corrigan was shot through the head, and with the one wild cry, fell to rise no more. It was evident to the men now that they had been duped, and that Vincent Lorraine had not been really absent from the castle. Hours had, therefore, been lost, and unless the breaking down of gates and doors could be accomplished with tolerable expedition there was great likelihood of the siege being raised by the arrival of constabulary in large force from Galway. But the men, it furious before, were mad with rage now, and deadly as the attack would be to the assailants, there was no idea of abandoning it. One man suggested starving out the landlord, but the others shook their heads. Mr. Lorraine was not the man to yield; and besides they did not know how long he could hold out, and it was impossible to maintain a long siege. But who would first "take in hand an axe" for the assault on the gate? The men looked at each other for a few moments in silence. Then Fergus Creagh, a tall powerful•man, said "I'll be the first, me bhoys. Now then, Bring° brae' h The axe whirled over his shoulder, came down upon the gate with a terrific blow, producing a deep dent, but no further impression. The men laughed. Creagh drew back swiftly for another blow; had half raised his arms, when suddenly arms and axe fell together. Creagh sprang up, tell, and rolled over, writhing, struck near the heart by a rifle bullet from the oak , room window.
"Another," said Vincent Lorraine, as coolly as if he had been practising in a shooting gallery. "Fergus Creagh is quit of his rent.
"Whit noble Lneurno comes next
To tart. our Roman eheerr" "They will make a combined rush,* said Hyacinth, under her breath.

Almost as she spoke Lorraine had laid down the rifle and the '"six-shooter" was in his hand. Hyacinth snatched up a pistol too. "Let me go to another window," she said. "No, no, Lorraine answered, quickly, "not out of my sight. If for a moraent you were seen they might fire! The very thought makes a coward of me. Stand so "—placing her ;—" now you can see the gate and cannot be seen."

Agitated voices, stibdned to muttering!, reached, them, but thmtv could not make oat words. In ten minutes the voices ceased, and from ,under the lea of the wall six Men sprang. Two, axe in hand, rushed to the gate, three levelled rifles at the oak room window and fired ; but the bullets whizzed harmlessly through the window and bedded themselves in the opposite , wall. Three rapid shots from Lorraine's revolver told with fatal effect; one of the "firing party," as he laughingly termed them, fell dead ; a second was wounded; the third fell on his face, and under cover of the smoke scrambled under the shelter of the wall. Hyacinth had aimed at the "gate party." Her weapon was a double-barrelled revolver; her Aid shot wounded the foremost of the two melt; as he reeled, back the second struck him, and he fell. A yell rose from the, remnant, and in an instant they disappeared. "Well done l" exclaimed Lorraine, turning with flashing eyes to his "lieutenant." "By Heaven, ,sweetheart, I never saw ,such steady firing from a ,woman's hand—such a fragile stripling, too; but do not /know well," laying down the pistol to take her in 'his arms for a moment, "how dauntless a soul lives in this tender frame."

The girl smiled, but trembled a little, t 400; and Lorraine would not have had it otherwise. However good the cause, however justly the life forfeited, no man would care to see a girl of eighteen shed blood as -coolly as a veteran._ _ _ _
What would be the next movement of the besiegers? This presently became apparent when there sudaenly appeared above the wall' something white on a long pole, and Lorraine burst out laughing.
"A flag of trace, as I live," be said ; the mouchoirat Sedan was nothing to this. So ho! they don't like such warm work.*

"Take care !" said Hyacinth, quickly, "it may be a feint—don't show yet.' 'Very comical looked the improvished emblem of peace, waving above the wall, and the besieged both laughed heartily, though softly—not wishing to be heard. Pistol in hand, Lorraine watched but the be- siegers had had too much of that terrible weapon to rashly brave it, and perhaps they did not feel quite cer- tain that M. Lorraine would understand what the white rag was meant for. " Misther Lorraine ! " cried a stentorian voice—the voice of Dermot Grady. . . . _

Back came the flute-like voice, only a little raised. "What have you to say, Dermot Grady?" " Whisht ?" muttered that personage. " I didn't think the spalpeen would reckignise me." He called again. "Will ye hear what we've got to say?" Yes, if your speaker shews himself unarmed! . . . .
A se'ranibling -sound followed this, and in a few moments the shaggy head a a yeung man appeared above the wall.

"'Tis Rory Maguire," whispered Hyacinth. "Dolly Maguire's son. Dolly holds tire acres of you." "Does she? She pays her rent, then, or I should have heard of her." He stepped forward in fultview of the herald of peaoe, and said coolly— " Say what you have to say quickly, Rory Maguire." He saw the man change countenance on hearing himself thus addressed by name. H 6 replied, howtver, at once.

anner, I've to say that all the bboys will go away an' not touch ye, if yell oonsint to lave us alone for this day's work, an' to lave the men^ye've sarved in howldings, an' forgive 4them the rint that's due, I an' take it down half for the toime to come."

"My good fellow," said Lorraine, smiling in genuine amusement, " youfllon't seem to know that a flag of truce usually means that the people sending it are not exactly in a position to dictate terms; but yonsould not ask more if you had gained a victory. If I decline your proposition, what then?" . .

Thin, yer anner, we'll bring a hundred more men, an' we'll take good earn ye don't git the sodgers up, an' when we've got into the castle, ye won't git no marcy." "Thank you. My answer is this: first, that every man who has taken part in this affair will pay for it with life or liberty, and each one is known by sight and name. secondly, that all or any of my tenants shewing sympathy with to-Jay's work will be sum- marily ejected, whether or no they are widows or fatherless; thirdly, that I give you two minutes to destend from your present position, and after two minutes I fire."

A fierce howl of rage and hatred greeting this un- compromising reply. It was clear that should the assassins fail in their object, they would be worse off now than before. They coufd hardly, indeed, expect ranch mercy from a more merciful man than Vincent Lorraine. Needless to say that Rory disappeared with remarkable celerity, and once more hurried consulta- tion was held as to future proceedings.

I Whenever the Government made a proposal likely to I benefit Ireland the Opposition supported it, but when ' the Government were engaged, as in the present year, in a course the most unwise and the most unconstitu- timal, in proposing coercion in Ireland in a manner likely to distutb and break up the foundations of social erder in that country, the Opposition did everything in. their power to encourage strict obedience to the, law, and ho believed that their respectful advice to the people of !roland had been of more use in procuring obedience than all the Government constabulary, inanaged as it was at Mitchelstown. He contended that it was im- possible to justify the proclamation of the Ennis meet- ing on the principle laid down by Lord Eldon. It was no answer to say when the law 'was tampered with, "You also did it." If the Liberal Government tampered with the law so much the worse and so much the more ; necessary was it that the practise of the Executive should be brought back to the law: What the Opposi- tion wanted was to drag the general doctrine of public ' meetings into view. In the case of the .Ennis meeting the Government had not even attempted to show that their proceedings were in conformity with the law laid down by the highest authorities. As to the Mitchels- town meeting, he thought the conduct of the Chief , Secretary appeared to be marked by singular rashness and imprudence. The debate was contirmed by the Attorney General for Ireland, Mr. Dillon, and Lord It Churchill. The Arrourmr-GiErnsitaf • for IRELAND defended the action of the Government in proclaiming the, Ennis meeting. Mr. Diffox asked why the meeting at Mitchelstown was' not proclaimed if the Government were aware beforehand that it. would be attended with illegality. Lord R. CHURCHILL said it would be difficult to find a precedent in Parliamentary history for the conduct which ex-Ministers had pursuod in bringing all the:weight of their influence to bear against the Executive. Mr. PARNELL moved the adjournment of the debate. --Mr. W. H. The Marquis of IxrrulArt, in moving the second read- ing of the Technical Schools (Scotland) Bill, gave a short history of the measure, in order to account for the late period of the session at which it came before their lord- ships. He explained that the reason for not postponing it to another session was that the triennial election of the Scotch School Boards took place next year, and to put off legislation till next session would, therefore, practic- ally have the effect IA delaying the operation of the Act for three years. Lord Lmonor entirely sympathised with the object of the bill, but it was a measure of the greatest importance, and he'regretted that when the Government separated the bills for England and Scotland, and dropped the Eng- lish bill, they did not also postpone the Scotch bill. The second reading was agreed to,the Committee stage was negatived, and the bill was read a third time and passed. WOMEN'S SUFFRAGE.

In answer to a question put by Mr. Lahouchere, on bshalf of Mr. Morley, Mr. BALroun Said the inquiry into the Belfast riot was conducted under an Act of Parlia- ment. without which no sworn inquiry could take place. The proceedings at Mitchelstown would probably he made a subject of judicial investigation, and it would be inconvenient and prejudicial to the ends of justice to have a concurrent inquiry proceeding. THE APPROPRIATION RILL - TREATMENT OF IRISH POLITICAL PRISONERS.

On the motion for the third reading of the Consolidated Vend Appropriation Bill; Mr. Cox, referring to the action of the Government under the Crimes Act, in proclaiming the meeting recently announced to be held in Ennis, said it was believed by the people of county Clare that the object oi the Government was to bring about a collision between the inhabitants of that county and the police and militia. It was, however, the resolve of the Clare people that for every meeting suppressed by the Govern- ment they would 'hold a dozen meetings which the Government would he unable to suppress. The hon. member also referred to the recent death of Head. Con- stable Whelan, for which he expressed his deep regret. Mr. Ihttox said it had become manifest that it was within the power of the Government to inflict personal punishment on their political opponents, and especially the, members of the Irish party, who, therefore, had a right, to demand. some security that they should not be treated as if they were pickpockets. His own experience was that the food was meted out on a starvation system, and as an instance of this he mentioned the case of a man whose health and appearance were im- mensely improved in the course of one week simply by the extra food which he (Mr. Dillon) and another prisoner were able to conceal for that person in a coal cellar.

• Mr. £.J. Ruvuma,' replying to Sir C. Lewis, said there were ample means of remedying on appeal any injustice that :night be alleged as to the action or the magistrates in the Portrush ease. THE BULGARIAN SITUATION.-ATTITUDE
THE POWERS.-A CRISIS IMMI-

NENT. • Penn, Mownst—The Journal des Debats publishes a telegram from Bucharest, dated yesterday, stating that M. Radoslavoff has been arrested on a charge of treason by order of M. Stambtdoff. Several fresh arrests have been made of Bulgarian officers. BRUSSELS, MONDAY.—A correspondent sends a telegram from Bucharest saying that, in political circles there, it is stated that Bulgaria will be occupied by a Roumanian army, and Roumania by Turkish troops. Sr. PETERSBURG, MONDAT.—According to information on the best authority the Turkish Ambassador here has been ordered to postpone his intended journey to the Crimea for the benefit of his health. The Turkish Government seems to be firmly convinced that fresh complications in the Buirtarian question are about to arise, which might make Shakir Pasha's presence neces- sary at any moment VIENNA, MONDAT.—Private news from St. Petersburg states that in political quarters the opinion prevails that Prince Bismarck in reality is not in favour of the expulsion of Prince Ferdinand from Bulgaria. At least, for Austria's sake, Germany might accept him as Regent. •

_ ODESSA, MONDAY.—Private telegrams from Sofia state that all the chances are now in favour of Prince Ferdin- and being re-elected with all the legal formalities on the absence a which, in the first election, Russia and other Powers based their opposition. VIENNA, TUESDAY.—A telegram from Sofia states that a great assembly gathered this morning in the court of the Cathedral, to denounne the conduct of M. Karayeloff. The crowd became very excited, and attacked M. Karaveloff's house, smashing the windows with sticks and stones. They then turned their attention to the office of the TirnowAka Constituti&n, which has un- reservedly opposed Prince Ferdinand, and treated this building as they had done that of the ex-Minister. The people then moved towards the place, and upon the Prince appearing at a balcony he was received with en- thusiastic and continued plaudits. When the applause had quieted, Prince Ferdinand briefly acknowledged the hearty greetings of the people, concluding a warm and appreciative speech with the cry of "Long live Bulgaria." The people then dispersed in good humour. Order has not been further disturbed.

div.p: NEWSIFROM MR IL M. STANLEY.

ST. PAUT. DIC LOANDA, SEPT. 9.—Major Barttelot, who was left at the camp at Yambunga. at the foot of the Aruwhimi rapids, with a garrison of about 100 men, has forwarded the following information to Leopoldville concerning Mr. H. M. Stanley's .expedition :—Major Barttelot received news from Mr. Stanley despatched about July 12, after he had made a ten days march from Yambunga towards the interior', Mr. Stanley was at that date still proceeding up the Arnwhimi. which he had found to be navigable up to a certain distance above the rapids. Here he launched a steel whale-boat which he had brought with him, as well as several rafts manu- factured. for the expedition, and which had been utilised for conveying the heavy baggage. All the members of gm expedition were in good health, and provisions were easily procurred in the large villages near the river. The country through which the expedition was passing showed a gradual rise towards some high table-lands. Another caravan of 480 men was following the expedition on the left bank of the Aruwhimi, the advanced guard, consisting of 40 Zanzibaris, under the command- of Lieutenant Stairs, being composed of men lightly burdened, whose duty was to search for provisions. Mr. Stanley hoped to arrive about July 22 in the centre of the Mabodi district, and expected to reach VVadelai in the middle of August. or even before. The advance had been so peacefully accomplished that Mr. 'Stanley had instructed Major Barttelot that, should it continue so, he would shortly send him orders to follow the expedition by the same route at the head of the 100 men left at Yambunga. Major I3arttelot had paid a visit to the Falls, accom- panied by Tippoo Tib, and had !eft a detachment of 20 men there. Tippoo Tib arrived at the Falls station on June 16.

CONFLICT AT MITCHELSTOWN. • THE KILLED AND MAIMED. __

1 The man .1-Ennia-,-li-n-geiTiiii ;i;;;;;;;CiOus all night. expired about ten o'clock on Saturday morning. His - hat has been.kept by his friends for production at the inquest. It is pierced right in the centre of the band by a buckshot or swan-shot, which cut a clean hole throu,gh , the felt and penetrated the brain. , It appears that there were $4 constables treated for 1 injuries of various kinds, about half of them for scalp . wounds received in the affray in the square from sticks and stones. Two inspectors lost their helmets in the , scrimmage and in the subsequent charee. 1 Constable Leahy, who was so severery beaten during the riot, is, though still very weak, coming round. His , depositions were taken, and he is able to identify a man, , named Gould, as having assaulted him. Gould is under i arrest. The police are able to identify quite a number of ; people who assaulted them, and numerous prosecutions i will arise out of the proeeedings of Friday. ; 1 The police version of Friday's outbreak gives a different ; complexion to the lamentable occurrence, when corn- ; pared with some of the published reports. They state . that when it was seen that the Nationalist leaders I intended speaking a stenographer was, in accordance . 1 with standing instructions' sent, forward, under escort, ;to take a shorthand, note of the speeches. The crowd, I which was chiefly composed of Tipperary "boys," armed ' 1 with blackthorn sticks, resisted the escort, and kept I them from reaching the plat form. 'Men some one from I among the the speakers shouted out, "Bold together, Iboys !" and the mob,talting, this for the signal for active resistance, closed in round thelittle band of 15policemen, i stoning and clubbing th'em 'without mercy. Up to that moment, the police declare their batons had not been used, but the constables were now compelled to fight for ' their lives, and, even when, by holding solidly together, they got dear of the crowd, the people still kept up the light—chasing the constables right Into the barracks and belabouring them'with shillelaelts and stoning them duritig the whole of the retreat., Every man among that escort of fifteen sustained Wounds of a more or less I serious nature. On arriving in the barracks, the police I state, the mob continued to throw stones, and, fearing I that, flushed with their success in having beaten back ' the escort, they would next attempt to carry the build- ing, a few blank cartridges were fired; but as the stone- • throwing still went on, and the attitude of the Mob be- came . more threatening, ball cartridge was used: Seeing that the riot was one of serious dimensions, it is declared that the police had no option but to clear the square; and as forty more constables were severely injured in carrying out this 'order, the police 1 authorities consider that fact alone proves that the.Tip- i perary and other contingents had come to Mitchelstown for the exnress nurriose of creating a riot. \ I . _ ANOTEiER DEATII.—THE_INQUEST. - -

A third death—that of the youth Casey—has resulted, *Om the Mitcheletown affray. The inquest on the three bodies was proceeded with on Wednesday. Head Constable Doherty, who was in charge of the constables sent to pro- tett the reporter, said that while he was making his way through the midst of the crowd he asked the people to "please make way for the reporter," but they paid no at- tention te his request. When his men had gone six yards a voice from, the platform cried out, "Keep close there; don't let them up any further," whereupon -the people raised their sticks and pushed the police hack, and also threw stones. The police were overpowered, and they re- -treated tOlheir barrack,- pursued and stoned by the mob. The witness then described the attack on the barrack. He could Rot sty whether an order to fire was given, but he saw the first shot fired by Sergeant Kirwan. It was not the. ease, as stated in the House of Commons by the Chief Sec- retary. that the barrack door was broken open before the first shot was fired. Counsel for the police said he admitted that there was no order for the first shot to be fired. The witness added that no persons were injured by the stones which came inside the barrack. Mr. John Conbrough, of Blanefield, Stirlingshire, who was on a tour in the neigh.' bourbood and witnessed the affair of Friday, said the crowd at the mecing was so dense that he thought at the time that the pence could not make their way to the platform. They could have got at the speakers by going round at the back of the waggonettes. The police were pressed back by the pressure of the crowd, and then they made an onslaught on the crowd He was not at the barrack when the first shot was fired, but he immediately afterwards saw six or eight rifles protruding from the barrack window' and there was certainly nothing like a crowd there then. His opinion was that the police were trying to break up the meeting. Cross-examined by counsel for the police, the witness pointed out Mr. Condon, M.P., as the person be saw on a waggonette pointing in the direction of the police, but he said the row began long before that incident, and, in answer to Mr. Harrington, he said that Mr. Condon was trying to quieten the people. The inquiry was adjourned to next day
MR. LAROUCHERE, _M.P.. AND THE POLICE
OUTRAGE.

Mr. Labouchere, M.P., spoke on Saturday night at %- great meeting held at Cork, under the auspices of the Yeung Ireland Society. Mr. Hooper, M.P., presided, and was supported by Messrs, Brunner, Ellis, Flynn, O'Hea, Lane, and Gill, Members of Parliament. The Chairman, iii opening the proceedings, said the men who were mas- sacred atMitcheistown were the latest martyrs to Irish freedom, and their names would live and their memories be revered when the names of their murderers would be remembered only for their infamies. Mr. Labouchere.' who was loudly cheered, denounced the action of thet Government in reference to the meeting at Mitchels- town, and said he did not hesitate to say that a more foul, more base, and more despicable Government never cursed a country. Describing what he had witnessed at' Mitchelstown, he maintained that the proceedings were quite orderly until the police attempted to force their way through the crowd, that the police assaulted the police in a cowardly. manner, and that the resort to fire- arms was most unjustifiable. The scoundrels and vil- lains who had dared to commit the murder in the public. streets should be severely punished. Messrs. Brunner and Ellis also denounced the conduct of the police. Mr. Labouchere writesto a London paper an account of the affray at Mitchelstown. After describing how the reporter and his escort attempted to force their. wog through the crowd, he says :—"By this time the re- porter, with his escort, was as near to the head of the brake as a member at the bar of the House of Commons is to the Speaker. One of the constabulary at this moment drew his bayonet and wounded one of the horses. The horse reared, on which two police- men batoned the rider. The escort with the reporter fell back on the main body of the police,, and all together rushed upon the crowd, right and left. At once sticks were raised, and there was a scrimmage, but as few of the crowd had thick sticks, and as few even of these could get at the police, the resis- tance was slight, but the police seemed to be as cowardly as they were brutal. After a minute or two they lied in disorder to their barracks, with the exception of Captain Seagrove. who ran like a hare to a neighbour- ing hotel, where he seems to have concealed himself for some time. Mr. Dillon jumped down from the brake and walked to the barracks in order to see, if possible, the head of the conatabulary, and to urge him to re- frain from further incitement to disorder. The door was closed, but on his knocking he was let in. He found the police in a wild state of exeitornent. They had dragged two men into the barracks mnd were bludgeoning them as they lay with their faces downwards. He describes the Chief Constable as almost beside himself, and in reply to repeated requests to keep his police within bounds he said he would march with his police. With the greatest 'difficulty indeed, by hanging on to his arms, Mr. Dillon prevented his rushing out with his men and shooting right and left. In conclusion. I assert that two men more unfit for their delicate duties than Captain Sea- grove and Mr. Brownrigg could not be found on the face of the globe. They are responsible for the deaths which took place. They by their bungling and bullying created the disturbance, and if every man had his deserts they would be sentiinced to a lengthy term of imprisonment.' ARREST CT MR. O'BRIEN.—EXTRAORDINARY

A small crowd which had assembled at Sackville street cheered Mr. O'Brien as he passed, and a larger crowd at the station greeted him with enthusiasm. There was tin time for further demonstration, as the train started almost immediately. _ _ _ _ _

Mr. O'Brien arrived at Limerick Junction at a quarter past ten, being greeted by the way with every demonstration of enthusiasm and respect At, Marybormigh a pretty large crowd was assembled, and after a local politician had entered Mr. O'Brien's car- riage, and addressed the people in denunciation of the hon. member's arrest, Mr. O'Brien spoke a few words. Ile declared that he never went upon a journey which would be I better for Ireland. The Government might close his lips, but they would never silence the feeling that was in the hearts of the Irish people for him. There was a spirit left in Ireland that all the bayonets of the Government would never silence. At this prat the local head constable and a subordinate entered the carriage, and at the former's request Mr. O'Brien desisted ' from firrther addressing the people. The train moved away amid cries of "God be with you," " Hurrah for Michelstown," and cheers for Mr. O'Brien. Contrary to expectation Mr. O'Brien was taken straight On to Cork, where lie was met at the station by the pr3minent citizens. The railway station and all the approaches were crowded, and a squadron of the 4th Hussars, a company of the Argyle 'Highlanders, and 2.00 police, all tinder the command of Captain Plunkett and Mr. Gardiner, It.M., Were drawn up in the station. Mr. O'Brien was conveyed in an outside car to the court- house, and was accompanied in the vehicle by the Mayor, the High Sheriff, and the Head Constable. The journey to; the Courthouse occupied an hour and n half, owing to the pressing crowd along the streets. .The Mayor was very active in keeping the crowd back, and promised Mr. Gardiner he would preserve the peace, and condemned the presence of the military and police as unnecessary, and calculated to irritate the people. He also complained that the step was taken without his being consulted. At the Police Court, after some formal evidence, Mr. O'Brien was committed to gaol, pending the trial at Mitchelstown. Trnnps and police escorting him to gaol were stoned. police charged the crowd, and,in the olilie which ensued, a number of policemen and specta- tors were injured.

IVhelehati; who was In plain clothes, remained °inside, the premises, and when the moonlighters entered five of them were made prisoners: On the police coming outside, li,wever, they found Whelehan lying dead in the field., Whelehan, who had been on duty at •Ennis for the last four years, Was married, and leaves five children. DUBLIN COITORATTON_AND_THE GOVERNMENT.

At Monday's.ineeting of the Dublin Corporation, the Lord Mayor, M.P., in the course of a lengthened speech. denounced the action of the Government with reference to the. Ballycoree and Mitchelstown meetings; describing their policy as one of terrorism and murderous violence. It was not the fault of the Government that there was no bloodshed at Ballycoree, and ten times more people. would have been injured at Mitchelstown but that many of them had blackthorn sticks in their hands. Ills lordship was of opinion that the matter should be re- ferred to a committee of the whole Council, suggesting that resolutions should be adopted Calling on all liberty. loving men to imist the'irish people in the present crisis, and approving of the speeches delivered by Mr. O'Brien at Mitchelstown, and for Which he has been prosecuted. . _ _

in the discussion that followed, Mr. Gregg, a Protes- tant. Heine Ruler, said though a man of peace, he was proud of the men of Mitchelstown, and he felt certain that if :he people had acted similarly elsewhere, the police would not !vivo been so ready with their bludgeons.— The Council then resolving itself into a committee, the tegolutions suggested! hy the Lord Mayor were carried, two members alone dissenting.
THE BOLTON STRIKE.-OPEN ARBI
TRATION ACCEPTED.

On Saturday a meeting of the engineers of Bolton was held in the Temperance Hall, for the purpose of con- sidering the offer of the employers of open arbitration on the wages question of the dispute. Over one thousand persons were present. Mr. Charles Hough, chairman of the Joint Trades Committee, presided, and there.were in attendance deputations from Manchester, Bury, Oldham, and Blackburn. After three hours' dis- cussion, a vote was taken by ballot with the following result :—For arbitration, subject to satisfactory details being arranged, 452; against, 267; majority for arbitra- tion, 185. The announcement of the figures was received with applause.—The Rev. Canon Atkinson, vicar of Bbl- :on and rural dean, was present, and expressed his pleasure at the nature of the vote arrived at. The de- cision will be communicated to the Masters' Association, and arrangements will then be made for satisfactory details. No reply has yet been received from the Home Secretary to the representations made to him by the deputation from the newly-formed Rate- payers' Association with regard to the expense the borough is being put to by the continued refection of the county constabulary. The county constabulary is, however, being gradually drafted from the town. There are none now stationed inside the works where the knobsticks are employed, although a number are kept constantly patrolling outside. So far as can be gathered—for the authorities refuse information—there are now about 80 special constables in the town. When the complaint was made to the Home Secretary a fort- night ago there were 200. The "knobsticks" are still looked upon with the greatest aversion, and when they venture out they are hooted, and, in some instances, assaulted. On Saturday several scenes of this descrip- tion occurred, and one man was apprehended for dis- orderly conduct. Four of the imported men who were molested whilst walking out last Sunday, have memo- rialised the Home Secretary for protection, and Mr. Matthews has communicated with the Mayor (Mr. Alder- man Fletcher) on the subject. It is computed that there are now over 300 imported men at themarions establish- ments, divided as follows :—Kay-street Works, 120; Soho Foundry, 110; Victoria Foundry, 70; Ryder Bros., Beehive Works, 7. At Bolton, on Monday, two cases arising out of the strike were heard before the Mayor and other magis- trates. In the first John Cooper Smith, striker at the Victoria Foundry, was committed to prison for seven days on a charge of intimitiat ing an imported man em- ployed at the same works by nsing threata.—Ernest Jones, apprentice at the Soho Foundry' was charged with assaulting, along with others not in Court, another imported man named Buckmaster, on Sunday afternoon, and was committed for 14 days. On Monday, the Joint Committee of the men issued a manifesto with reference to the vote taken on Saturday afternoon, whereby the strike hands resolved to accept "open arbitration" as a basis of settlement The com- mittee say that whilst accepting the vote as decisive they reserve to themselves the right of arranging the details Upon which the arbitrators shall act, so that they do not surrender any right hitherto possessed by them. A meeting will be held this week to arrange details for the arbitration. The employors' secretary has given an undertaking to stop the importation of workmen pend- ing negotiations. The men continue to receive generous support, Cork having sent its first contribution, viz., £1.0: Dublin (second). £6 Ills.: and Burnley (first).-

FOOTBALL. . • 4 RUGBY RULES. WARRINGTON (J. E. WARRISN'S TRA/d) T. WERNETH.—. Ti e epening match of tbe season of the latter club was played on Saturday, wheu Mr. J. E. Warren, the Warring- ton secretary, was invited to take a scratch team to com- mence their winter pastime. Several of the team originally selected found it difficult to make the journey, for Jolley, Massey, and Fair Turner were conspicuous by their absence. Excellent substitutes, however, were found in Antrobns, Bandies, and Evans. The latter, who played with remark- able dash, will not lack notice in the future. The game was strictly confined to the forwards. as it was blowing almost a gale when the teams arrived on the ground to commence hostilities, good passing being out of the question. War- rington were placed at a great disadvantage soon after the start, for Barnes was compelled to retire owing to an acci- dent. He came on again at half time, but was of little or no use. The caused Handles ro fall out of the forward ranks, and take the vacant position bshind. Two thirty-fives hav- ing been agreed on, Frank Turner started the oval, and a good return being made by M Askton, the first scrimmage was formed in Warrington quarters. On the ball becoming loom, the borne team rushed the leather to the line, whores pass from Haigh to Ashton (Werneth) resulted in that player kicking in touch-in-goal, scoring first blood for Wer- neth. Turner dropped out, and smart following up by Littlewood and Povev prevented a return, play settling down in Werneth territory. Give and take play followed, until the visitors broke away in a grand dribble, resulting in Tomlinson touching down. Wood dropped out, and a smart run by Warren and a good pass to Barnes was foiled by the wind carrying the ball forward. From the scrim- mage Speakman passed to Warren, who put in a good kick, this being responded to by Coop, but Barnes replied, and from this Davies got over. The try was, however, dis- allowed, owing to same informality. The Warringtonians, not to be denied, pressed severely, and from (Male loose kicking Mosfley had his kick charged down by Frank Tur- ner, which enabled that player to scare the first try fer the visitors. The place was most difficult, and Barnes failed to improve on it. Haigh re-started, and Evans pot in a good run, but was well tackled by Moseley. The visitors' for- wards now rushed the ball over the line, and lomlinson sived by kicking dead. Haigh dropped out, and a dodgy ran by Buxton settled play in the cen- tre. A good pass by Antrobus to Barnes enabled that player to make a splendid run, but on being tackled by Moseley the former pleyer here met the accident as reported above. A good tun and kick by Warren placed play in the home quartets, but the Werneth forwards retaliated by a good dribble, Speakman saving. From the scrimmage Wheratt passed to Mayers, and from a grand dribble by the home team they scald a second minor. Ralf time was shortly afterwards called, leaving the score Warrington one try and two minors te Werneth two minors: On changing ends E. Fitton put the ball is inetion, and play settled in the visitors' territory. From a scrimmage, Wood kicked dead. Turner re-started, and Moseley failed to return, being tackled by Ashton. The Weneth forwards rushed down the field, Warren saving by touching down. Turner dropped out, and smart following up on the part of Rigby, Levies, and Littlewood prevented a return. From some loose play, the ball was rushed over the Warrington line, and Buxton kicked dead. On the oval being brought out, some pretty paesieg by Speakman, Warren Barnes, and Evans settled play in the home team's lines, Warren, ultimately touching down. On the drop out the Werneth forwards again broke away, but this rush was epleudidly stopped by Warren, whom saving tactics at this point of the game were perfection. Not to be denied they took the ball over the line, and Buxton saved. Turner re-started, and Moseley returned, scoring another touch down. A good pass was made by Speakman to Warren and by the latter to Evans, who looked like sc 4ring, but was well tackled by Meseley. The Worneth men played strongly, and a rueh by Moseley almost scored, only being brought doin on the line, Buxton saving. A free kick was allowed Warrington for off side tackling, and exchange kicking between Evans and Tomlinson brouebt play in centre fieldovhere no side was called, with the score War- rington 1 try three minors to Warneth 7 minors. The play was, not of the best description,owing to thehigh wind which prevailed. Accurate passing was nut of question, and the visitors' team was severely handicapped owing to their have. log to play short-handed when the game was in its infancy. Of the backs, Buxton was safe, and let no opportunities pass; Barnes was playing a grand game until be retired ; Evans was promising, his coolnees and Judgment being ad- mirable. Warren played with his old dash, whilst the halves both played a safe game. The forwards worked hard, Davies, Littlewood, and Frank Turner deserving special mention. For Werneth Moseley, E Fitton, Buckley, and Tomlinson played well. The following were the teams : Warrington : J Buxton, full back ; J B Warren (captain), T Barnes, and J W Evans, threequarter Lacks ; W Speak- man and J Adtrobus, half backs; H Ashton, Frank Turner, W Dillon, R Littlewood, T Davies, W Hayes, W Puvey, J Rigby, and E Bandies, forwards. Werneth : Tomlinson, full back ; Moseley, M Ashton, and Coop, threequarters ; Whyatt and C Haigh. half hacks; Clarke, A Wood, J Wood; E Fitton, F Fitton, Mayete, Shorebridgs, Kent, and Buckley, forwards.

Mr. W. O'Brien, M.P., was arrested at seven on Sunday evening, while bidding good-bye, on the mail steamer to Mr. Labouchere, M.P., and Mr. Brunner, M.P., on their departure for England to take part in the debate on the Mitchelstown affair. Mr. O'Brien had been asked by some of his colleagues to go over to England, also to take a share in the debate, but he decided not to go, but to await the expected arrest in Dublin. He accordingly remained in the city all day, his movements being watched by detectives; and in the afternoon he went with Dr. Kenny, M.P., to dine with Mr. John Dillon at the latter's house at Ballybrack, near Kingstown. The whole party was engaged in conversation on board the steamer, when Superintendent Reddy, the chief of the detective department of the Dublin police, accompanied by Sergeant Cooper, went on board, and the former, beckoning to Mr. Harrington, called him aside, and some- thing like the following conversation took place : Superintendent Reddy : I beg your pardon, Mr. Har- rington, I would like to say a few words to Mr. O'Brien; have some business with him. . .

Mr. Harrington : Well, he is here, but whatever busi- ness you have you must do yourself. I shall, of course, not facilitate you in any way. Superintendent Reddy: But I have important business with Mr. O'Brien, as I believe he, is going away to Eng- land to-night. . _ -

_ Mr. Harrington : I repeat that I cannot help you in any way; you must do your business yourself. Superintendent Reddy showed Mr. Harrington a copy of the warrant he had in his hand for the arrest of Mr. O'Brien. It was signed by Captain Stokes and Mr. Itatou, resident maiistratei at Mitchelstolps, and emus.

THE EXETER DrISASTER,-THE IN- QUEST. " ANOTHER DEATH.

. ...... Another death waa yesterday added to those previously announced in connection with the fire at Exeter Theatre, a man named George-Woods, steward of the Exeter and County Club, having died in the hospital, Another.suf- ferer is in a critical condition. •

A strange incident occurred on *Friday last, during the search among the debris of the pit. In one corner was seen to be standing a youth. ' Ile was upright, the eyes and mouth were open, or partially so. enough to strike the observer. Men went tip to the body to remove it, as it had been their melancholy duty to do with so many others, when the lad crumbled to dust. What could be picked up was reverentially plackfOn a suitable vessel, and removed to the lower mortuaiyi, Mr. J. F. ElListon, proprietor Of tho nOlton and Black- ourn Theatres Royal, organised four' performances on Friday for the benefit of the sufferers by the Exeter theatre fire. These were—Mr. T. W. Robertson's "Ours," at Bolton; and Messrs. Wynn Miller and Ellisten's "Mv Sweetheart, at Blackpool; "Alone in London," at Bel- fast; and "In the Ranks," at Belfast. As a result £lOO will be forwarded to the relief fund.

' The inquest upon the bodies of those who were burnt in the fire at Exeter Theatre was resumed on Monday. the coroner being assisted by Capt. Shaw, C. 8., as repre- senting the Home Office. The Coroner explained the course the inquiry would take. -First, he should receive the evidence of those who were within the theatre, and afterwards lie would take scientific evidence as td the construction of the building. At the outset it was discovered that the members of the "Romany Rye" Company, who were sunimoned. had gone to Portsmouth, despite the fact that they had been warned uot to leave the city, and had promised not to do so. _

_ The Coroner, amidst expressions of approval, woke strongly with regard to this breach 'of agree- ment and contempt, and intimated that as these per- formers were those who could give the very evidence the jury were wanting, they had shown, not merely a want of respect for the court. but is want of appreciation of the duty they themselves owed to the public. An order was given n ofli ivaenthacterltwierol vdriftentecsisietshserld attend when required, or Evidence to correct mistaken identity having been given photographs of the building, and a copy of the Act Of Parliament under which theatres were licensed, were produced. The Town Clerk said all the. Town Connell could do was to make provision for the stability of the building. The Magistrates' Clerk said that the justices examined the plans, with the assistance of the City Surveyor. They suggested various alterations, which Were pro- mised, and the magistrates then Intimated that if the theatre were erected precisely in accordance with the amended plans, there would be no objection to the license. The magistrate had no power over the structure, but they suggested a second exit from the gallery, and also that a window at the head of the gallery steps should be converted into a door. Neither suggestion was adopted. On tlie nigtit of the fire there was a post in the centre of the gallery stairs. That was not there when the magistrates granted the license. They would have objected to anything of the kind being placed in the theatre, ono of the rules being that there should be no obstruction, either permanent or temporary. Numerous suggestions that the justices did make were, adopted. A post and a door in the gallery steps had 'been fixed without any communica- tion with the justices on the part of anyone connected with the theatre.—A juryman said the post narrowed the exit from the gallery to 3ft. 51n.

At the adjourned inquest, on Tuesday, the Borough Surveyor said although, the Town Council had a hy.law regulating the entrance to and exit from public buildings, yet when the theatre plan came before the committee they were advised that these by-laws could not be ea- forced, the Public Health Act net giving the power the ' by-law assumed. The Council had no authority beyond seeing to the stability and the sanitary arrangements of the building. The alterations required under these heads were made. He accompanied the justices in their inspection, and made several suggestions, but felt that he was exceeding his province! Be quite expected to find an iron curtain, and was disappointed at one not being there. The barrier constructed in the gallery stairs was contrary to that shown in the plan. The doors between the stage and the theatre were not fire- proof, so that even had there been an iron curtain, the fire might have found its way into the auditorium through the stage floor and doom. He was never in- structed by anyone to make an offipial inspection and report on the theatre.—ln further evidence it was stated that three obstructions had been placed on the gallery stairs that were'not there when the magistrates licensed the theatre. One of these was a door 4ft. 6in., in a pass- age but a little over 511. wide, as. that when it swung out It almost entirely blocked the I horotighfare. The two exits from the upper circle were but 311. din, wide. .One-fifth of the people in the circle were burned. There were believed to have been two fires, one which flashed up the gallery stairs, and the other which gradually burned the build- ing. The London Theatre Regulations were handed the Theatre secretary, and returned by the architect with Lhe Intimation that. they had all been anticipated. The theatre would hold 1.200 iv On Wednesday the inquiry into the circumstances at. tending the recent disaster at the Exeter Theatre was re- sumed. The Mayor of Exeter stated that so far as tke city justices were concerned they were desirous that the inquiry should be of the most searching character. The Coroner said he was strongly of opinion that the licensing magis- trates should be represented by counsel or otherwise, and 1 the Mayor replied that he would at once consult with the justices. Members of the Romany. Rye Company were then called to give evidence, and the inquiry was again adjourned. On Thursday morning, at the reopening of the inquest on the victims of the Ore at the Exeter Theatre, the Mayor laid the magistrates had met and considered the suggestion

div.head: SARAH BERNHARDT'S IMMENSE RECEIPTS AND PATTI'S PERIL . . . .
div.p: SARAH BERNHARDT'S IMMENSE RECEIPTS AND PATTI'S PERIL . . . .

Sarah Bernhardt's receipts, for her late tour in South America, are the largest ever taken by any dramatic artiste. But the reckless Sarah scarcely ever has a franc to spare! Patti has also aChieved great success, and a very large amount of money, in Mexico and South America, but came very near being the victim of a dynamiter who attempted to throw an explosive bomb at her while she was singing at the Grand Opera House in San Francisco, California. She was called again and again in front of the curtain when, as she was finally retiring, a Irma in the gallery suddenly rose, picked up a bomb from under the seat, and raising it in the air, was about to throw it, when it exploded in his hand, shattering his arm and face, and inflicting other injuries. Had the man net placed himself under the protection of a policeman, who met him as he was rushing down stairs, he would have been torn in pieces by the in- furiated people. Patti displayed great coolness and pres- ence of mind, and succeeded in restoring quiet by singing "Home, Sweet Home." Poor Patti! It is a wonder she was not killed by the nervous shock, or that she did not faint, or that her hair did not turn gray through fright. Think of Patti with gray hair! A beautiful bead of hair is the crowning glory of woman, and its loss is her greatest misfortune—a mis- fortune which may be prevented by the use of that famous hair restorer and dressing, known as Mrs. S. A. Allen's World's Hair Restorer, which will prevent baldness and restore gray hair to its natural color, strength and gloss. It can be had at any chemist's or perfumer's shop in the civilized world.
Instruction's were received at Sheerneae, on Thuredav, for her Majesty's ship Forester to proceed to Lowestoft to strengthen the fleet employed in protecting the British North Sea fisheries.

°RENT FIRE IN BusstA.—At Nevel, in the Vilebsk go- vernment, in Russia, a great fire took place on Wednesday. More than 100 houses have been burned to the ground, and a dozen persons perished In the flames. A few minutes before eleven o'clock on Thursday morn- ing a fire broke out in the mixing room of Firth and Sturdy's Bankfield Mill, Blackburn, containing 50,000 spindles. Damage to the extent of £l,OOO has been done. A few evenings ago Douglas House, Petersham, occupied bmyrsM Fajooas Major Foe, was peon:seersesdedbyhai rnt ghei le; ,wof jewellery valued at finding his way to upwards of £2,000. No arrest has been made. WASHED OVERBOARD.—The steamship Britannic brought news to Queenstown on Thursday that during the late hm- ricane in the Atlantic the captain and helmsman of the IBritish schooner William Jones were washed overboard and drowned. STrnid TO DEATH —A retired former named Massom, re- siding at Little Crosby, near Liverpool, died early on Thurs- day morning under singular circumstances. He went out on Wednesday evening into his garden to take a hive of bees, when he was attacked by them, and severely stung about the head and face. He would have been 74 on Thurs- day.
