div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 17, 1887.

THE beginning of the end" of the agi- tation for making the Warrington library a Free Lending Library may now be said to be visible to every eye. We have all along con- tended that the Library and Museum Corn- thitttee were acting illegally in lending books to one section of ratepayers whilst denying I them to another. Last weetc we wrote—" The ratepayers, one ard all, stand before the law Upon an equal footing; and we say emphati- cally and advisedly that the committee are I •breaking the law in a most outrageous man- her in using what should be a Free Public Library as a Subscription Library." This , Week the opinion thus expressed is con- finned by the statem .nt of Her Majesty's Attorney-General. In the House of Com- mons on Tuesday evening, Mr. BRADLAUGH put the following question. He said— " beg to ask whether under the Public Libraries Act, 1855, the Warrington Library and Museum Committee are justified in requiring and receiving subscriptions from persons borrowing books from the Warrington Free Library, which is supported from the rates; and whether the committee are legally justified in according privileges to subscri- bers in respect of the loan of books from the Free Library which are not accorded to ratepayers who do not pay special subscriptions." The answer of the ATTORNEY-GENERAL Was as follows "There is no authority under the tublic Libraries Act of 1855, for making any distinction between Persons who subscribe and persons who do not. In Iny opinion the Act does not contemplate the loan Of books out of the library, and I think it doubtful whether such loan is legal. Assuming, however, that, under section 21, rules could be made permit- ting the loan of books, it would, in my opinion, be enropetent for the committee to require a reasonable deposit to ensure their safe return." It is IO be hoped that, after this authoritative Pronouncement, there will be no attempt, so far as the.Warrington Library Committee are concerned, to evade the obligation which lies Upon them to remedy the wrong they have been committing for over thirty years, by im- mediately taking steps to make the institution free in the lending as in the reference depart- 'tient. The subscribers have no locus slandi ; they never have had a legal footing since the Libraries Act was adopted; there is no

authority under the Act, as the ATTORNEY- PENERAL says for "making any distinction °etween persons who subscribe and persons Who do not." But the Committee have them- selves made this distinction ; and they have thereby broken the law. They have trampled, 30 to speak, upon an Act of Parliament ; they are offenders of the most flairrant kind, for they have continued to offend in spite of Dated warnings. Still there is no desire to visit their sins upon their heads ; they have ly to turn to the right path—to set about "40ing the right thing, and we dare say they I'M be forgiven. It will be observed that the ATTORNEY-GENE- /IAL, while emphatic in stating that subscribers as such are not entitled to any privileges, ex- Presses a doubt as to whether it is legal to lend books at all; but suggests that if books 4a.re lent, it would be competent, under sec- "On 21, .6 to require a reasonable deposit to etitlsure their safe return." With regard to I.9is, we may say that, acting under the sec- in question, nine-tenths of the Free f ibraries in existence in this country have nd a better way than the one suggested ensuring the return of books. The usual r°tlrse is, when a burgess becomes a bor- i°Wer, for him to fill up a form of voucher, .ri„ Which he undertakes to become respon- ;.te.le for any loss the Corporation may SUS- by loss by loss or damage of any book in his , izvtlssession. A ratepayer who is on the but- Ss roll is found from experience to be b good " for the value of the book he may h:trow• If, however, the borrower does not thl)Pen to ba a voter, he is required to get 0: signature of a burgess, who undertakes, a his behalf, to guarantee the Corporation Rai nst any loss. The process is simple anrgh : it is found to work admirably; OW it is much better than requiring a bor- be er to furnish a deposit. The Act, it may irkr_enlarked, makes no mention of a deposit 1.47 section in question (2 i) gives the Com- 'tee authority to " make rules and reuula-

tions for the safety and use of the Libraries and !Museums and Schools, and for the admission of the public." The regulation adopted may, of course, insist on a deposit, or it may be take the more common, and, as it seems to us, more desirable form of a voucher. As regards the doubt which the ATTORNEY- GENERAL has expressed as to the legality of lending books, we think any hesitation on that head may be dismissed in view of the way out, which he himself suggests, and in view, too, of the fact that, from the time of the passing of the Act to the present day —that is, more than thirty years since—it has been the custom to lend books, under the Act, by nearly every Free Library in the Kingdom. The original Libraries Act was passed in 1850 ; but it was repealed to give place to the amended Act of 1855. Man- chester was the first town to adopt the Act. The Manchester Free Library was opened in September of 1852, DICKENS, THACK- ERAY, and other eminent men taking part in the proceedings. Books were lent out im- mediately, for we find from the returns that the total issue for the first year was 138,312 —being 61,080 in the Reference Library, and 77,232 in the Lending Library. The total issue at the present time is more than ten times this number ; it is, roundly speaking, one mil- lion and a half. A hundred other towns have acted in a similar way, and with simi- lar results. There is no going back. Sir JOHN LUBBOCK is trying to get a bill through Parliament to extend Lending Libraries to villages as well as towns. Warrington is not a village, although it is afflicted with some village notions ; it is a town which has adopted the Act, and, having adopted it, must carry it out in its entirety.

THE National Association for the Pro- motion of Technical Education is going to work in the right way in seeking to obtain in- formation as to the needs of various localities, and of the persons who are willing to lend a helping hand in carrying out the work. It was hoped that the Technical Instruction Bill would become law this year; but the Government were too much interested in making mischief in Ireland to have sufficient care for the working classes in England. The bill has been dropped ; but it will in all pro- bability be revived and carried next year. Meantime it is highly desirable that local branches of the new Association should be formed in every industrial centre with a view to collecting information, and ensuring that the measure, when placed upon the statute book, shall be one that in every respect meets the requirements of the times. If this be done, it may not, after all, be a disadvantage to wait a year. The bill which the Govern- ment had in hand was not one that could be regarded as final; it was open to several ob- jections ; but it may be that the difficulties which were in its way will be got rid of if they are grappled with during the recess. Lord HARTINGTON has been appointed president of the Association, Sir JOHN LUBBOCK treasurer, and the secretaries are Sir H. E. ROSCOE and Mr. A. H. D. ACLAND, M.P. We have received a communication from the Secretaries, in which they say : We should be very much obliged to you if you could kindly give us the names of any persons in your town or district who are interested in Tech- nical, Commercial, or Agricultural Education, and who would be willing (quite apart from any pledge of pecuniary support) to give us advice as to the work of the Association, and the means by which we may make it most useful in your neighbourhood. As we are also anxious to procure as complete infor- mation as possible of what is actually being done for technical education at the present time in the United Kingdom, could you give us the names of those who might be willing and able to give us such ,1 information in connection with your district? Instead of collecting the names ourselves and forwarding them, we have thought it better to I, let those who are interested put themselves in communication with Mr. ACLAND (35, Cado- gan Terrace, London, S.W.), who is the acting secretary. It would be brtter still, of course, if some leading inhabitant in each town would take upon himself to convene a meeting of men of kindred views and character, with a view to forming a standing committee. There is much.to do in the matter of preparing the way before a system of technical education, such as is proposed. can be worked successfully in connection with the elementary education now being ' given in our national schools. Towns like Runcorn and Widnes would have to turn their attention morn especially to instructiofi in connection with the chemical trade; St. Helens and Prescot would, in addition, have to look to skilful training in the manufacture of glass and of watches; Earlestown would need to see to the best methods Df construct- ing • locomotives; while Warrington would re- quire to direct its attention not only to glass land chemicals, but to acquiring special skill in producing iron, wire, leather, cotton, and 1 soap. There is a wide field, and the labourers lin it are as yet comparatively few. Those who get soonest to work are, it is hardly necessary to say. most likely to keep ahead; for a good start is a great advantage in the race for technical knowledge, as in every , other race.

PARLIAMENT has been occupied during the week with the discussion of the murderous conduct of the Irish police at Mit chelstown. It would seem, judging from the statement of Mr. LABOUCHERE, Mr. BRUNNER, Mr. ELLIS, and other credible persons who were present when the fatal conflict ensued, that the con- duct of the constabulary was utterly indefen- sible, and that they ought to be put upon their trial for the murder of the people who were killed with shots from their rifles. The meeting, it should be remembered, was not a proclaimed meeting; it was a legal gather- ing, and was being peaceably conducted until the police broke in upon the assembly. Their object was, it appears, to force a re- porter through the crowd, in order that he might take notes of the speeches; and the meeting not unnaturally resented this intru- sion. Government reporters, as Mr. GLAD- STONE stated in the House on Monday, have no rights beyond those of ordinary citizens; and, this being so, it follows that the police had no authority to try to find him a place by breaking through the meeting. They , were in a similar position to what a body of Liberals would be who sought to force , a way through a Tory meeting with the ob- ject of getting one of their number on the platform as a speaker. Those who were be- ing pushed aside would have a right to resist—the natural right to resist aggression. Because, in the Mitchelstown case, the in- truders were policemen, it does not justify their conduct; it rather aggravates it, seeing that they are drilled in some knowledge of the law and orderly behaviour. The police- men were pushed back, and then they be- gan to use their staves. The people struck back, and the policemen ran off to the bar- racks. Here the matter should have ended, but the constabulary, thirsting for revenge, took up their rifles, and the result was that many innocent persons were injured, two

The magistrates at Newton Petty Sessions on S.aturnay had before them a case of alleged railway travelling without paying the fare ; but when it was about to be zone into they were struck of a heap by the objection that they were all more or less interested in the case as shareholders in the London and North-Western Railway Company. It was found that tht re was ground for the objection against all the justices then present, and the case was adjourned, so that it might be heard by another bench. It is one thing, it seems, to qualify as a magistrate, and another to qualify for a particular case.

div.head: 'TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: 'TOUCH AND GO."

Several of the members of the Warring- ton Cycling Club seem to have come a bad cropper in the race for the championship. Wheeling is like matrimony—it has its ups and downs ; it is a case of weal or woe.

Now that the football season has com- menced, it is to be hoped each player will enter into a solemn engagement with him- self to play in a gentlemanly way—win or lose. As to kicking, they must take Mark Twain's advice, and "Punch, brothers, punch, but punch with care."

The smoker is hard hit. He pays an enormous duty on his luxury; tobacco wouldn't, in fact, be a third its present price if it were duty free. And now it has been discovered that some manufacturers adulterate with moisture to the extent of more than one third. Let the lover of the weed put that in his pipe and smoke it.

The death of a boy from hydrophobia, at Lowton, has led the magistrates at Newton to issue an order for the confinement of dogs in that division until the 3 st October. Happily, cases of hydrophobia are rare, but the disease is such a horrible one—and so frequently fatal-.—that the magistrates are more than justified in ordering dogs to be confined.

A contemporary says :—" Readers can do us good service by mentioning the name of the paper whenever they are led to make purchases or inquiries owing to advertisements which appear in these colums." In other words, people must pay for advertising in the paper, alter which they are requested to ad- vertise the paper for nothing.

An attempt is being made to settle the Cass case. and on Wednesday the trial was postponed until next sessions. Miss Cass has recently got married, and Endacatt's solicitor urges that this being the case "no injustice could result to her." But this is " not good enough." The offence is one against society as well as the lady, and it will be a grave mis- carriage of justice if severe punishment is not inflicted upon the offender.

Mr. Beamont, of Orford Hall, Warring- ton, has now reached his ninetieth year, and he keeps in good health. It is absurd, how- ever, to say, in the words of a contemporary, that "age has not enfeebled his bright and vigorous mind." Those who come in con- tact with him know that he ha 3 aged mentally and physically these last few years. Still he is a wonderful old man—for his age, and we trust he will live to complete the cycle of a century of years.

Warrington Grammar School has been undergoing enlargement and impiovement to meet the requirements of the largely increased number of pupils. But it requires to be im- proved altogether; it should be removed to a more suitable site. The town has so grown that at present it is at the " back of beyond:" and it is lost at times in the smoke of Messrs. Rylands' works. It would be a good thing for the Rev. E. J. Willcocks if he could be furnished with a new school where there is less smoke. A word to those who are rich as well as wise should be sufficient.

The Americans seem to have caught a Tartar in the English sparrow. They gave him a welcome years ago, and now they shower curses on him. He is a great eater of corn, and is looked upon as allied to " the devil's own." Tne Ornithologist

of the United States Government proposes to make it a misdemeanour to give him food or shelter. We should say " Poor Sparrow r but we know he will be equal to the attacks on him. And then, as Shakespeare has it, "He that doth the ravens feed" will " Pro- vidently cater for the sparrow."

The member for the Northwich Division of Cheshire is amongst the English members who are making a gallant stand in Ireland on behalf of the Irish. He is qualifying, as he put it, for a plank bed. Under the Coer- cion Act—so villianous is it—he could be run in already for having, •as two resident magis- trates might say. "incited to the terror of Her Majesty's subjects." But the Govern- ment, like most bullying people, are cowards; they da not dare to enforce the law against an English member.

Sir William Harcourt made a splendid defence, on Monday night. of the right of public meeting and showed that the present Government were worse in their action than in the worst days of the worst Governments. It was a revelation when he stated that when Lord Spencer was Lord Lieutenant of Ire- land, "there never was a public meeting about to be held in Ireland which the land- lords did not beg the authorities to suppress." How suggestive! These landlords are afraid of a light being thrown upon their doing, because they know their deeds are evil.

The Runcorn Board of Guardians are not satisfied with the way in which the River Weaver Navigation Company do business They "want to know, you know," and have decided to appoint a committee to make in- quiries. Mr. Aaron said " they had earls, dukes, and lords who knew no more about the Weaver Trust than pigs." Really, it is shock mg to speak of "real live lords " in this way. Mr. Aaron must thank his stars he is not in Ireland, or he might have to lie on a pjank bed. And, then, is he not hard on the pigs? There have been several learned pigs in the land.

RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH.—It has been arranged that this church shall be re-painted and cleaned throughout, the contract for the work having been given to Mr T, Kirkham. of Runcorn.

"JACK" BRIGGS.—ThiI well-known Widnts cricketer left home on Monday to proceed for Australia. Briggs sails with the English team to-day (Saturday). CONJURING ENTERTAINIIPNT AT RUNCORN.—Mr. Hartly, an illusionist, has this week been /appearing at Runcom Public Hall. anl hii entertainmtnta have been very well attended. DYSENTERY AT WIDNES,—Mr. Dictem, nuisance inepec• for, has drawn up ra truort which Allow,' that during July there were two deaths from dysentery, sod in August there w,re eight deaths in Wirtnee. Hutchins ,n and Co, fell into a vat of caustic liquor, and had his right leg badly scalded. He is in a serious condition.

HARVEST THANKSGIVING SERVICES AT WIDNES.—On Thursday a service of harvest thanksgiving was held in connection with St Paul's Church, which was tastefully decorated. Among those who assisted in the decorations were Mrs Deacon, Mr H Wade Deacon. J.P., Mrs Hoole, Mrs James Williams, Mrs Deakin, Messrs Beach. Neil, Imison, Moss (Halebank). Thomas Baker (Bold), Smith (Appleton), and Brookes; and the helpers, the Misses Deacon, Mrs J Mrs J R Jones. The Rev A Maitland Wood, MA., vicar of Runcorn, preached a sermon appropriate to the occasion. he collec- tion realised the earn of £5. TROTTING HANDICAV AT WIDNES —The final heat in con- nection with this handicap, which had to be run again 11 consequence of a dispute, has resulted as follows :—lst, Mr. George Davidson's Hector, 280 yards start; 2nd, Mr. Twigge's Stole-away, 100 yards. Mr. Quinn's brown mare did not again compete, owing to having suffered from lame- ness since the last race. The heat, which was run in 4nnins. 25secs., Hector winning •-asily, was witnessed by a large number of persons.—On Thursday afternoon a trotting match took place on Bold•road, near Widnes, between Mr. JAWS Smirt's "Silence " and Mr. J. Scrlyeee " Ju-t in time," for a stake of LW. There was a large number of spectators. The distance travelled was two miles, Sctiven to receive 100 yards start. The betting was 6 to 4 on "Silence," which was driven by Mr. Halligan, of Liver. pots'. "Silence," gaining on its oppinent, caught up in the first mile, and won easily by ten yards. A STARVING Intstntax.—an Iris's farm I tbourel, named Michael (iarrey, was brought up in custody at itunc.trn Police Court on Tuesday on a charge of having stolen a scrubbing brush and an umbrella, value 3s. the property of a farm bailiff named Walter Taylor, of Marsh Gate Farm, Sutton Weaver. Prosecutor is bailiff to Mr. Chadwick, and on the 2nd instant the articles were missed, and Sergeant Oldfield deposed to having his attention drawn to Mr. Acton's farm at Sutton on the 3-d instant by the bark of a dog. He saw the prisoner, whose face was blackened, mak- ing an attempt to raise the sash of one of the windows. He arreated him, and found the missing brush in his possession. Prisoner also had the umbtella, and on being asked to give an account of how he got the articles gave various evasive answes, On passing Mr Taylor's house he admitted hav- ing stolen the articles, and pleaded that starvation was the cause of his guilt. Ho was sent to Knutsford gaol for 14 days. RUNCORN BCRIAL BOARD.—The manthly meeting of this body was held at the office at the cemetery, on Wednesday. Mr. Rogerson presiding. The fellowing members were also present :—Messrs. Handley, Colebnrn, Whittaker, Littler, and S. Taylor, with the Secretary (Mr. Sal keld). The inter- ments for the past five months ending August 25 Is were 126, as compared with 116 for the corresponding period of last year, being an increase of 10. The fees received for the same period amounted to £l4l 9a 21, compared with £l2O 2s in the corresponding period of last year, being an h•crease of £2l 7s 2.l.—Mr. Handley reported that a meeting of the Finance Committee was held that day, and it was stated that the fees received during August amounted to £55 15A 81. The wages paid amounted to £l2 5s 6.1, leaving a balance in hand of £43 10a 21. HI31; DEATH RATH AT WIDNES. During last mooth the death rate for Widnes was 37 per 1 000 of the popula- tion. JOHN EUWARDS —The re- mains of the late Mr. John Edwards, who for many years was postmaster at the SimMs Cross office, Widnee, were interred on Tuesday afternoon at Farnworth churchyard. The deceased died on Friday evening, after a short but severe attack of dysentery. Mr. Edwards had also held a position as foreman at Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co.'s works, a post which he hadheld for a long time. A large number of the workpeople attended the funeral. BRUNSWICK BOYS' SCHOOL, Rutecoarr.—The report of Her Majesty's Inspector shows that this school has earned an excellent merit grant, or obtained the mark excellent for the year. Considerably more grant has been earned than the Education Department is allowed by Parliament to pay. In addition to this, excellent " was obtained for drawing'. No school in Cheshire, up to July last, had got excellent, which speaks well for the Brunswick School, which ha q had two excellent reports in one year. . . . .

A TwELVE DAYS' MtsstoN.—On Sunday the Rev. Thos. Waugh, the well-known Connexional Evangelist, com- menced a twelve days' misiioa at Widnes, in the Victoria- toad Wesleyan Chapel. The proceedings commenced on that day at seven o'clock in tke morning, when there was a prayer meeting. SUCCESS OF A WIDNES ATRLETE.—J. Carney, of Widnes, who had 89 yards start, ran first in his heat in the Shef- field Doncaster Handicap, the opening heats of which were run off on Saturday afternoon at Newhall Grounds, Shef- field. He beat F. Campbell, of Selkirk, 89 yar.is ; Corn- field, of Walsall, 91; and F. Morris, Alcester, 861, winning by a yard. On Monday Carney followed up his success by winning his heat in the second round, but failed to gain premier honours in the deciding heat, which resulted as follows :—Broadbenr, Oldham, 1 ; Walker, Notts, 2, Tatter- sall, Glitberoe, 3; Carney, Widnes, 4. They were on a voyage from Runcorn to Limerick with coal, when on Saturday morning the schooner foundered in the channel, about thirty mike north-east of Copeland Island. The captain and crew took to their boat, and were subsequently picked up by the schooner Bohemian Girl of Belfast, in which they were con- Yeyed to that port. A MISSING BOY AT WIDNES.—The Widnes police have for the last day or two been grappling the canal, near Messrs. Gossage's works, in the hopes of bringing to the surface the body of a boy named Thomas Roscoe, son of Mr Thomas Roscoe, of Church•street. The missing boy left home on Thursday evening week, and the same day was seen on the canal bank apposite Meeers.Gonsage's works fish- ing, but has not since been heard of; and as his cap was on the day following found in the canal about 300 yards from where he was seen on Thursday. it is thought that he has been drowned. Uo to the present the efforts of the police have been ineffective. and no intelligence has been received up to yesterday concerning him. STABBED By A PENCIL.—A girl named Annie Beesley, who is about ten years old, whe lives with her parents in Cross-street, Widnes, is suffering from the effects of a pe- culiar accident. She was running across the street, carrying a blacklead pencil in her hand, when she slipped and fell. On her being picked up, it was found that the pencil had been broken in the fall, and that a portien of it. passing through the child's clothes, had penetrated the flesh. She was at once taken home, and was thence taken to the Sur- gery of Dr. McCambridge, where the lead, which had pene- trated to a depth of three Inches, was extracted by Mr. Burgess. who is assistant to Dr. McCambridge. Great pain was suffered by the girl, but she is row recovering from the effects of the accident. _ _ .

FRUIT BANQUET —O3 Mrnday evening a fruit banquet was held in connection with Ellesmere-street United M, diet Free Free Church, Runcorn, and the occasion was made more interesting by a concert, in which the choir, assisted by members of the Mutual Improvement Class, took part. During an interval fruit was distributed. The chaie was occupied by Mr. I. Stubbs, who mild that their friends had been exceedingly kind in sending so large a quantity of fruit. He paid a high c...mpliment to the chotr, who, he said. had always shown a willingness to assist in church matters, mod he was sure they had done a great clod to- wards helping to clear off a laTe amount of debt at ode time and another. Th.re were many things to clear off yet, and no doubt every effort would be made to accomplish what was desired. lie hoped that the same concord and unity would exist around them in the future as had been noticeable in the past. After stating that the Mutual Im- provement Class bad had a successful career last year, he concluded by explaining the advantages to tra derived by young men who joined the dens. A pleasant evening was spent. RUNCORN INDUSTRIAL BUILDING SOCIETY.— The fifth appropriation meeting of this society was held in the National School, Runcorn, on Wedneedey evening. There was a good attendance of members. Mr. Albert Jordan, the chairman of the Board, presided, and explained that in ac- cordance with their desire to have an appropriation by bale lot and sale alternately, and the previous appropriation having been by sale, the present one would be by ballot. The balloting was accordingly proceeded with, resulting in No. Mt belonging to Mr. J. W. U. Glover, being drawn. Mr. Glover being clear on the socieiy's books, was therefore declared entitled to an advanca of £2OO free of interest.— The Chairman said that the next business was the appoint. meet of a solicitor to the society. Their late solicitor. Mr. Oliver Leak, owing to his removal from the town, bad re- signed. Letters were read from Mr. F. A. Lake and Mr. W. D. Jolliffe, anplying for the appointment, and also agreeing to accept an amended scale of fees. These gentle- men having been duly nominated for the vacancy their names were put to the vote, resulting in Mr. Lake be- ing elected as solicitor to the society by a majority of 17 votes.

PRESENTATION TO A POLICE INSPECTOR.—At the Police Station, Leigh, on Thursday, Superintendent Weir, on behalf of himself and other police officers of the Warrington Division, presented a handsome marble timepiece to Inspector Robert Charnley, on the occasion of his retirement from the force after upwards of 31 years service. The testimonial was subscribed for by the whole of the officers without exception, testifying to Inspector Charnley's popularity. Thanks to the visitors closed a pleasant meeting at ten p.m. CARDINAL MANNING AND THE DRINK TRAFFIC.—A great convention in connection with Cardinal Man- ning's League of the Cross was held on Wednesday, at Newcastle-on-Tyne, Father Nugent, Liverpool, presiding. There were delegates present from London, Liverpool, Manchester, Lancaster, Black- burn, Dublin, and Glasgow. A letter was read from Cardinal Manning,who said it was an immense joy to see the rapid and solid growth of the League of the Cross in England, and the still more rapid and solid growth in Ireland. The work of Father Matthew, the true and only founder of the League, was re- vived in our day, and upon them would the future of that work depend. They were not only fighting against intemperance, but against the great trade which made people intemperate, lie had never used hard words against brewers or distillers, but against their trade. They grew rich by increasing the selling of intoxicatihg drink, which destroyed men and women and children, and wrecked the homes and domestic life of the land. There would never be in the land the atrocities that blackened London and all populous cities if parents were sober and their homes pure. He begged them, therefore, first to do all in their power to help the United Kingdom Alliance in its efforts to obtain local option, or the local veto, by which people would be able to defend themselves and their homes; second, to bring up their children from their infancy in total abstinence from all intoxicating drink ; and lastly, to do all in their power to persuade temper- ate and good people who had never been tempted by excess to enter the League of the Cross.—Resolutions were unanimously adopted in favour of temperance legislation.

Churton. coroner, h-44 an inquest at the Commercial Hotel, at Frodsham, on view of the body of a man named John Woodc ick, bf Frodsham, who was 54 years of age. From the evidence it appeared that the landlord of the Commer- cial Hotel secompinied the deceased home at his request a few minutes after nine o'clock, and about half-pist nine o'clock Mrs Webb, a neighbour, saw the deceased lying on the floor of the kitchen with his head under the grate. With assistance an entrance was made through the window, the door,being locked, and upon lifting up the deceased it was found that he was quite dead. District Inspector Roughen, ef the county Kilkenny force of the Royal Irish Constabulary, has resigned as a protest, it is stated, against the recent action of the police. A convention of Irish landlords was held at Dublin, on Toursday, which passed a resolution repudiating in the strongest terms charges of neglect of duty and levying ex- cessive rent. At Bow-street Police Court, London. on Wednesday. Harry Wilkes, a telegraphist, was remanded on a charge of having altered certain racing telegrams sent by a news agency from Sandown last Friday. SUICIDE OF A MAGISTRATE.—Mr. John W. Brought, of Whigsbrough House. near Birr, a magistrate for King's County. committed suicide on Wednesday by blowing out his brains with a gun. A coroner's jury on Wednesday night returned a verdict that deceased committed suicide Whilst suffering from temporary insinity. A long Manifesto has been Issued by the Comte de Paris to the representatives of the Monarchical party in France. It is expected that the French Government will upon the earliest opportunity explain the policy which it intends to pursue during the coming session of Parliament, and thus reply indirectly to the Manifesto. ALLEGED MURDER or Two WOMEN.— A sailor giving the name of Theodor Quirain, but whose name is supposed to be August Nagel, has been arrested at Cardiff on a charge of murdering two women in South Germany eight years ago. The prisoner was arrested on the information of the German Consul at Cardiff, acting on intelligence received from the German Consul at West Hartlepool.

div.p: " IT ISN'T LEGAL."

Sir,—So it isn't legal after all, and your ccntention has been right from the first. Judge of my surprise, wnen I opened my "Daily Post" this morning, to find that Mr. Bradlaugb, of all the men in the world, had been asking the Attorney-Gaoral the sinie question that YOU have been ask. lug for the last twelve or eighteen months. And "so the Public Libraries' Act loes not mike any distinction be- tween persons subscribing and persons not subscribing." Just so, and that is as it ought to be, with a rate supported library. lam a little curious to know how Messrs. Web- ster arid Beamont and their confreres will feel about this matter now. But fancy them getting their coup de grace at the hands of Mr. Bradlaugh. That was surely the un- kindest cut of all. I shall await with no little interest the further development of this important question.—Yours truly, September 14th, 1887.
JOHN GANDY.
BRIDGE STREET BLUNDER.-A SUGGESTIC,Y:

Sir.-1 have lately been struck with the thought whether it would uot be wise for the Town Council to make an entrance into Stanley-street, across the vacant plot in Bridge- strcet, andto carry Stanley-street through into Bold-street. Every year we are reminded that the road round Arpley btati.rn is private property, and here is an opportunity which may uot occur again, of making a public thorough- fare whlch would be of great utility. I should alsS like to suggest that the Town Coursed should follow the example of the Manchester Corporation respecting the land in Bridge-street, and erect thereon a series of strops and offices similar to those erected in the City of Cotton. As the Corporation wont sell the land they had better make some use of it, and I can see no better use thaa the one I have suggested. Any way they ought to do soint•thing, and thus try to restore to the thoroughfare some of the trade which their blundering has destroyed.—l are. rEc., SUGGESTER.

div.head: FREE LIBRARY.
div.p: A FREE LIBRARY.

Sir,—A strong objection is often raised by the opponents of Ws increasing popular movement, that when books are permitted to get into the hands of the prOlic they quickly become soiled and offensive. As a subscriber to the Library, I should like to point out that present conditions do not by any means safeguard in this direction the borrowing mem- ber of dainty susceptibilities. My course of reading is rather mixed, and, as a relief from heavier literature, lam just now treating myself to a little fiction. The volume I have now on loan is of the" trashy novel" class, and it condition is almost repulsive. Besides a greasy ar.d soiled appearance generally, the book reeks so strongly with the stale fumes of tobacco, that my wife, who is also inclined to read it, cannot bear it near her. Personally I attach no weight to the objection that books of this character became rapidly the worse in a free lending library. I take it that the de. generacy of condition is directly proportionate to the use which has been made of the book ; i.e., to the number of times it has been read. Rather, than, should we rejoice to ncte that a volume has so soon fulfilled its mission, and concern ourselves only with the question of the ways and means of its early replacemenr.—Vours, &c., A SUPPORTER OF THE MOVEMENT.

div.head: WARRINGTON PARK WALL.
div.p: WARRINGTON PARK WALL.

_ . Bile—When it was announced that one of the objects of the local Jubilee Fund was the removal of the Park Wall, I maintained that the wall would never come down through that agency, and subsequent events have justified the opinion I held. It is useless to allow, or think of al- lowing, private individuals to do public works, and the none- this opinion is generally held, the better. Warring- ton suffers, and has long suffered, from such grandmotherly actions, and it is about time the inhabitant began to repu- diate such fostering care and to strike out for themselves. The removal of the Park Wall is a town's matter, and no single individual ought to have been asked to contribute a penny towards it. Every ratepayer should contribute his share towards the cost, and I am sure if a vote were taken up on the subject, there would be a majority in favour of the wall being demolished. It seems some of our Liberal council- lors think the removal of the wall is a persenal scheme on the part of the Conservatives because the Tory Club is built opposite the Town Hall, and consequently these Liberals have made a dead set against its removal. lam ashamed of such illiberal Councillors, and the more so as they hove no better argument in their favour than the old, everlasting Tory plea of no neceisity." Think of such Toryism from pro- fessed Liberals! No necessity, indeed ! Why there is every necessity. An elevated public taste den,ane.s it. The wall is a perfect eyesore, and has been for many years. We managed to put up with it when it enclosed the grounds of a private individual, who was afraid of his house being seen, but now it is intolerable. Now that the place belongs to the Town, let it be seen by the ueople, and let them have the freest access to it. If I had my way I would have entrances every thirty or forty yards all round the place instead of the obscure out-of-the-way islets there are at present. The plea of privacy is ridiculous. The Town Hall and Park were never intended to be a private asylum, but for the benefit of the townspeople, who should not be incon- venienced as at present. It is time we freed ourselves of this selfish, exclusive spirit, and cultivated a more gene- rous, trustful disposition towards our fellows. How many hundreds of our townspeople, who have no time to fre- quent the park, daily pass under the wall and are depressed by its gloominess, whereas, were the wall removed, the sight of the grass would refresh them, and they might de- rive many lessons of ocouragement in watching the growth and development of nature. Considering the great public benefit to be derived from the demolition of the wall, the question of cost should not be entertained, and I trust urn Liberal representatives will soon see the matter in its true light.—Youre,&c., A LIBERAL.

WARRINGTON FREE (?) LIBRARY. Sir,—The auawer of Alderman Webster on the Free Library question, at the last Council meeting, if nothing else is certainly oracular, and as is usual with such answers, It might and ought to have been considerably clearer and more to the point. Sec. 6 of the Public Libraries Act, 1850—the original Act —says that all books which may be presented to or pur- chased for any library shall be held upon trust for the benefit of the inhabitants of the borough. It will be noted that the books are not to be held for the upper, middle, or lower class, nor for those who can pay, or for those who cannot pay, but for the inhabitants, 2.e., all the inhabitants who wish to have the benefit of them. The Act of IMO has been repealed; but it is useful as showing the original
EEO

intention of those who framed it. By the Act at present in force—tnat of 1855—it is provided that the book and all other property shall be vested in "the Mayor, aldermen, and burgesses." Tte Library Committee are not even trustees of the ratepayers' property. Sec. 25 of the Act sass that admission to each libraries shall be free of all charge. Possibly it may be a nice goes- tiOn what "admission " means. if we are to take it in its literal sense, a person might be allowed to enter the library premises and then denied the use of any book therein can- tamed, and this would be admission, but certainly not the admission contemplated by the Act. Is is not evident that the Legislature meant that the word " admission" should be taken to include, not only bodily entrance into the building, but the enjoyment of all privileges and facilities which the governing hotly have provided, and which are paid for out of a common fund, viz , the library rate? No doubt the Town Council or the Library Committe e have, under sec. 21 of the Act, provided rules for the govern- ment of the library which restrict the lending of books to such persons as pay a subscription. Now it is well-known that a bye-law to be good must be equal and reasonable in its application and any bye-law which does not answer these (amongst (Aber) reqnirements is invalid; but the effect of a regulation that books shall only be lent to such persons as pay subscriptions is altogether unequal in its application, and both unreasonable and unjust, besides being in direct contravention of the whole tenour of the Act. It Ur' to a man who has money in his pocket "Yoe may have a book on loae," but to another who has no mosey it says "You shall not have one." And this although the library is repu- ted to be free, and is supported by means of the rate authorised by the Act. A practical mode of raising the question would be to at- tend before the auditor and object to the allowance of the items of expenditure in the library accounts, on the teround that the money has not been expended in accordance with the provisions of the statute. Possibly he, or, at any rate, the Court of Queen's Bench, might take a view of the law on the matter somewhat different to that taken by Mr. Alderman Webster and the Town Clerk.—Yours, ate., 15. h September. 1887
THE LIBRARY QUESTION.

div.head: / v v THE FXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEP EMBER 17 1887:
div.p: / v v THE FXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEP EMBER 17 1887:

sanctioned and enpaorteri by law. Opinion is free, and a man may hold what 0010108 he like, let it be sever 80 wild and baseless. Bat if lam told by someone that the Ship Canal has been made, and I go to the place where the Cinal is to b•, and find that not a sod has been mated, I conclude that my informant is entirely mistaken. As there ' is no accoutring for the vagaries of the human relied, I may not doubt that he is really of the opinion that the canal has been made. but I am sitifi-!tl that his opinion is based on delusion. So, when we are told by Alderman Webeter or the Town Clerk that in their opinion it is legal to debar ratepayers, by means of a subscription, from the tree of a library which is almost entirely impported by the rites we do not doubt that that is their opinion; but we turn to the Acts which regulate lierarlea of this kind and we do not find anything to supoort such an opinion. The necessary clauses or sections are as non-existent as the canal in the supposition I have just made. Alderman ‘Yelaster is asked in the Council to say upon what he founds his opinion, and what in his reply but a mere re-statement of the opinion. Could anything be more lame and Impotent, or more riclicu- •lously evasive? Either Alderman Webster &Ida he is in Ia corner and cannot answer the qaes:on he is alesired to answer without exposing his nakedness,. F. to speak, or he manifesis a lamentable intellectual inability to grace!) the matter that is really in dispute. Bat, sir. as I have said before, it is the Town Connell which really controls the-library, and it is with the Council that the reepentiNlity for the present mode of conducting the institutioe ultimaMly rests. There are many memhers of the Council wha, I believe, are not crinyinc.,d of the ex- peiiency of freeing the library, but who would not willingly have any part in infringing the law. These gentlemen must, after the reply of Alderman Webster. begin to sus- pect that the library is not on such a strong legal founda- tion as they might wish. They have seen distinct and un- equivocal charges made that the present mode of carrying on the library is not sanctioned by law, and they have Alderman Webster asked to show his legal credentials, if one might PO Pat it, and they have witnessed how com- pletely he failed to do so. And, what is more, they know that the interpretation put upon the Libraries Act in War- rington has not been accepted by any other tows. Unless we are disposed to maintain that Warrington is the only place in the kingdom where the law can he properly con- strued, this is evidence of the very strongest description. When Iva consider the long and keen struggle there has been in many towns before the Llbraries AG a were adopted and that the opposition has been nearly always based on the matter of expense, it is easy to understand what a strong temptation them would always be to adopt such a method of levying subscriptions as is pravised in Warrington in ceder to partly relieve the rates. Bait in no case does this course seem to have been taken. What is the obvious in- ference then, but that it was generally agreed that the law did not countenance any such method ? In conclusion, I can but expreme the hope that this question will again ba taken no at the next meeting of the Council, and that the representatives of the Library Committee will deal with it in a candid straightforward manner.—Yours. A RATEPAYER, Warrington. September 13th, 1887.

The CHAIRMAN celled attention to a case of relief that had come before him that morning. He said a woman with two children had come for some temporary relief owing to her husband being in the borough hospital suffering from an infectious disease. He wished to know in what position they would be in if that woman was affected with disease, as she possibly might be. They had no accommodation for infectious cress at the Workhouse, yet be understood that owing to the wife having received relief and become a pauper they would refuse to receive her at the hospital where her husband is.—Mr. JOLLBY thought that paupers were taken in at the borough hospital on condition that the Guardians paid something.—The Criatumale t No, not paupers.—Mr. HARRISON said that infectious cases, whether pauper or not, must be taken into the hospital in the in- terests of the town.—The Cmataistarr said that Mr. liar- bourne, the relieving officer, told him that if they took such a case as he bad referred to to the hospital Dr Gornall would not receive tier because she was a pauper.—Mr. JOLLRY thought Mr. Harbourne was under a misapprehen- sion as to that. He understood that any case or infectious disease, whether pauper or not, rich or poor, within the radius of the borough would be taken into the hospital.— Mr. HARBOUR/4H was at this point c tiled into the room, and in answer to the Chairman, said that if such a case of in- fection as that referred te by the chairman were to occur, he anticipated that there would be difficulty in the way of getting it into tbe borough hospital.—Mr. JOLLEY thought that if the case were taken to the borough hospital it would not be refused entrance.—The CHAIRMAN; If they did refuse it would be very hard on the patient.—Mr. HAR- BOIIRNH said it was only a short time since Dr. Gornall took the advice of the Town Clerk, and it was decided that pau- per cases should not be taken.—The CLERK said that might be so with regard to a tramp, or any case of that sort, bat with regard to any person whose house was rated in War- rington they could not say that such a person was not to enjoy a hospital which they helped to pay for in their rate. —Mr. HARRISON said the object of raising that hospital was to secure the safety of the people of Warrington, but if a case was refused admittance the consequence might be that the diseato would spread and affect the health of some other people who were paying rates. He would like to know if such a thing happened what sort ef heavy responsi- bility would fall upon the persons at that hospital. Ho thought they would be bound to take cases in.—The Gluon- NAN said that if that was the case the Corporation should instruct their officers accordingly.—Mr. VOISEY thought that some understandinz should be arrived at: for he under- stood that sickness was rather prevalent just now.—Mr. BLACWRIIRST suggested that Mr. aarrison and Mr. Jolley should brisk( the matter be'ore the Town Council, of which they were members —Mr. ISHERWOOD remarked that an- cording to the bye-laws of the Corporation it was the duty of the officials of the Corporation to remove these infectious cases.—The imbject then dropped.

FINANCIAL POSITION OF TIP% UNION. The CLERIC made an interesting statement with respect to the financial affairs of the Union, from which we give some extracts. He said :—The estimate of contributions required for the half-year ending Lady Day, 1888, was for- mally submitted to your Board at the previous meeting. I Ox upon figures to provide for a total capital aid of which sum, laowever, I esti nate a balance to be in the treasurer's hands, at the clone of the present half-year of £3,114. Application of this balance to the credit of town- ships leaves the present proposed actual call at £9,052, compared with £10,123 contributed for the corresponding half of last year, and .210,108 for the current half-year. The calls upon townships are, therefore, less by more than £lOOO than the average of the two last calls male. The estimated al propriation of the capital so to be provided is as follows :—Separate charges, £188; common charges, £8,125; county rates, £2,499; to meet expenditure before another call can be made, £1,354; total, £12,160.

With this report is produced the book containing al half. yearly financial statements from 1867. These statements show all sums received and paid, balances appropriated, nod outstanding liabilities in the 20 years. Comparison of the figures with the parish acoouots (particulars of charges, against each township, and lists of indoor and outdoor poor being half yearly sent to overeners) may easily be made.. The only continuous outstanding liability is that of the loan accotnat. The financial statement ending at Lady Day, 18722 (the half year preceding INV appoietenent as clerk), shows an outstanding loan of £3,037 10s to be due to the Public Works Loan Commissioners. At Michaelmee, 1875, the sem owing was £2,400; at Lady Day, 1878. £2,962; No. 1' loan from the Metropolitan Life Assurance Seciety,for 2882, having hen obtained. At Lady Day, 1850, the balance was £2,472 as Ti ; and at Michaelmas, £12,459 148 7d ; No. 2 lore for £lO,OOO having been obtained, At Lady Day, 1882. £11,963 18a 9d ; at Michael. coos, £15,267 15s ; No. 3 loan for £4,000 having been obtained. At Michaelmas, 1885, £14511 16. 91; and at Lady Day, 1888, £15,971 Sc 3d; No. 4 loan for .22,404 having been obtained. The four sums burrowed were paid by the lenders to the London agents of your treasurer, who disbursed them on the order of your Board thus—No. 1;2682 in payment te Mr. W. J. Legh for pur- chase of land; of the Nos 2 and 3, £lO,OOO and £4 0001 loans, a sum of 213,338 18e 8d was paid for land and build- ings at Iv:ideate, and £B4B 13s 7d for furniture, dm. (thel details of such expenditure were ordered by your Board to be printed in 2834, and copies thereof will be supplied to Guardians since elected). The balance of £l9 12s 9d has since been reduced to £4 us. £1,400 of the No. 4 loan of £2,400 was paid to the Public Works Loan Commissioners in discharge of the loan existing prior to 1872-2785 to Messrs. Collin and eon, and £39 5s to Mr. Owen, leaving a balance in the hands of your treasurer of £175 15s. It is desirable when outlay thereof in ac- cordance with the orders of the Local Government Board is practicable that the two balances of £4 us and £175 In be used and the accounts permanently closed. Your Assessment Committee fix the assessable value of ratable property for all local and to a considerable extent for Imperial purposes. The borough of Warrieg ton forms your chief ur/san district, within which the greatest progress ought to be found, or the signs of progress are not encourag- ing. The Rhumb Treasurer has added to his always care- fully prepared report upon receipts and expenditure a re- I turn, that may be accepted as accurate, showing the assess- able yalne and rates levied in the 30 years-1857 to 1886 An average total annual rate of about 5s 104 in the 2 I. there shown. Probably the sewer rates were, in the earlier years, small district rates, but they may fairly be adopted to show averages. It is, however, important to coasidar the analogies existing between values fixed upon property I generally in the first ten years, for rating purposes, and those I subsequently obtaining. Comparison of ratebooks would probably disclose material increases generally, and, in some cases, of wholly unaltered and structurally unimproved tenements ; instances of a double or even treble value would be met with, and we may well consider how far 9 past re- vision and increase of assessments for rating imposes made under favourable and much improving conditions will, in the possible absence of such conditions, be found practicable. The Union Assessment Committee Acts were passed in 1882, and, without doubting abnormal progress in the actual value and number of rateable tenements in the years 1867 to 1878. the work of the cbmmittee, and of the county Finance Committee,. bad in that period material eff-cts upon the system of assesentent before prevailing. The Borough Treastrer's return shows that whereas the total increase of ratable value in the first ten years was tinder £lO,OOO, that of the following tea years exceeded £35,000. Yet, again, in the succeeding and last ten years the increase fell to a sum tinder .217,000. What ie, however, of more serious impor- tance ie that with an outstanding liability (not, however, taken from the Treasurer's report, which' is, not before me when. writing this) of £272,000, a considerable portion of which I assume to be permanent annuities not subject to re- demption, after annual progression from 1857 (with one slight exception probably attributable to revision of the previone year's increase) the values fall thus: 1883, £132,684 ; 1884, £131,941 ; 1883, £131,133; 1888, £129,898. Similar examination of the financial position of other portions of your Unlen having separate local authori- ties May properly be made, for it is needless to say that falling sources of revenue with increasing liabilities are subjects for earnest thought. It is probable that the con- nection of the' Cheshire townships in your Union (formerly forming pact of the Runcorn Union) may also require to come under your censideration if any attempt is made to limit boundaries to those of the counties.—lt was agreed that the report should be printed for circulation. This was the chiaf business.

RABIES II; DOOR : EXTRAORDINARY INCOMMENDATION9. —The report of the Select Committee on Rabies in Dogs was issued on Saturday. The Cmunittee recommend CL) that when rabies is pi-evarent the muzzle should be en- forced; (2) that the power of the Privy Council should be extended to authorise the slaughter of stray dogs; that the symptoms of rabies shoMrl be endorsed on dog licenses; (4) that local authorities 4iou/d have power to order that dogs shoula wear badges which may identify their owners; (5) that. in populous places local authorities should place restrictions upon dogs generally, and especially deal stringently ;with apparently owner- less dogs in their districts; and (6) that in the event of its being conclusively proved that M. Pasteur's system provides a yreventive remedy, facilities should be afforded for its application in England.

STATUE TO THE LATE MR. lII7OH MASON.—A bronze statue, which has been erected by public subscription to the memory of the late Mr. Hush Mason, was on Satur- day publicly unveiled at Ashton-under-Lyne, and handed over to the Mayor as the representative of the Corpora- tion. The unveiling of the statue was made the occasion of considerable public rejoicing and ceremony. A. pro- cession, headed by the Mayor (Alderman Wilson), Mr. Addison, Q.C., M.P., the members of the Corporation and of the Memorial Committee, walked through the main streets of the town, which were decorated with flags and banners. A huge crowd assembled to witness the pro- ceedings. Mrs. Hugh Mason unveiled the monument %mid cheers, and Mr. A. E. Revner, the chairman of the Testimonial Committee, asked the Mayor's formal acceptance of it on behalf of the town. Mr. Addison, M.P., afterwards moved a vote of thanks to the Mayor, and the proceedings ended. THE CARLISLE TIIAGEDY: VERDICT OF WILFUL MURDER. —On Saturday Mr. .1. H. Brown, coroner, held an inquest at Carlisle on the body of Isabella Steele, aged 3 years, daughter of Mary Steele, belonging to Old Cumnock, Ayrshire, who was kicked to death on Thursday on the roadside, near to the Baffles,, Carlisle, by a tramping blacksmith, named William Hunter. belonging to Man- chester. The man, after killing the child, attempted to commit suicide by cutting his throat he is now recover- ing slowly. The mother of the child stated that Hunter had frequently beaten the child with his fists and also with a stick. Before he gave the child the fatal kick he had struck it on the side clf the head with his clenched fist, saying, " be hung far you.* The woman ex- plained that she had left Hunter that morning to go to her home, as he was always ill-using the child, and he had followed her on the way. The lodging-house people with whom the prisoner and the child and its mother stayed when they were in Carlisle said that the man and woman used to put the child into the wash-house there, and they bad to turn Steele and the man away from the house for the usage which both of them gave the child. The medical evidence showed that the body sad arms were one mass of bruises The head and neck were also much bruised, and these injuries were sufficient to cause death.--The jury wore of opinion that the child died from injuries inflicted by Hunter, against whom they returned a verdict of wilful murder.

Vast crowds were present • eight thousand prizes were given in sports, the child prizes being by the, Prince of Wales, the Duke of Edinboto,' Lord Rosebery, and other noblemen. There are also circus entertainments, concerts, balloon ascents, &e. Tho weather Was dull and threatening.

ATTEMPTED MURDER RY JUSTICE • OP THE PEACR—A Jug e de Pair named Dalgravois in custody at Pont St. Maxence for attempting to. murder a process-server, named Potencier, who had served a Writ upon him. He lay in wait for his victim,and felled him •to the ground with a sledge hammer. The blow, aimed at the head, took effect on the man's shoulder.. lie was dreadfully injured, and is not likely to recover. The Royalist papers are making political capital out of the incident, and point out that this. JUstice of the Peace was ap- pointed to his post by a Republican Minister of Justice.

THE TELEPHONE IN Om:A.—The Chinese look with atprehension at telegraphs, and onito recently it was reported that a telegraph line was destroyed in China because it was a "diabolical European invention." No such objection is charged against, the telephone, and no American syndicate is said to have received a contract for th& construction of important lines of telephones. Owing to the difficulty, bin; of adapting the telegraph to the 4,000 characters of the-Chinese-language, a vast ex- tension of the telephone-system the country is deeme,l probable. .

Ms INTRUNATIONAL INEETROUGIFT CONORESS, —An International Freethought Congress—at which delegates attended from France i Belgium, Italy, Spain, and llol- land--was opened on Saturday by Mr. Bradlaugh, at the Hall of Science, Old-street, London. In the after- noon and evening the Congress had the follOwingsubject under discussion--" Secular education. Ought the teach- ing to be neutral in the sense of indifferentism to reli- gious dogmas, or ought it to be distinctly hostile to religious b.,liefs?" The Congress by a large majority voted in favour of its being neutral in the sense of indif- ferentism to religious dogmas rather than being hostile. Tire MILH SErerty or LARGE Towxs.—On 'Monday a conference of Cheshire dairy farmers was held at Dun- hamin order to take into consideration the price to be asked for the winters supply of milk to the great towns. Mr: Jefferson presided. A communication was read from the Warrington Farmers' Club, urging them To appoint delegates to attend a great conference of milk producers at Manchester, and subsequently such a depu- tation was selected. /t was unanimously decided, that Cheshire farmers should ask, in the case of twelve months' bargains,. 2s. 6d. per dozen quarts Tor the six winter months, and 2s. per dozen for the six summer months. In case the bargain was solely for the winter months the price to be asked is 2s. .9d. per dozen quarts. The meeting instructed their delegates to Manchester to bring up the subject of excessive railway rates for the carnage of milk.

THREATENED EARTHWAREi—RaIph Falb, the Leipsie earthquake theorist, has written a letter in which lie calls attention to recent seismic coincidences that seem to confirm his hypothesis that earthquakes depend Imuch for their intensity on the nearness of the !won to the earth. He especially dwells on the great earthquake on June 9th, at VVerny, in Russian Turkestan, in which 328 men lost their lives. Shocks more or less violent con- tinued to occur till the end of July, when they ceased altogether; but oh August 22nd, three days after the solar eclipse, and two after the moon's perigee, a succes- sion of violent shocks, occurred which almost equalled the original convulsion. He concludes his letter by say- ing that the next critical days will be the 17th of Sep- tember and the 2nd and 16th of October. On the first day mentioned there will be strong atmospheric, perhaps terrestrial, disturbance. On the second day the disturb- ance will be less violent; but it threatens to be very serious on the 16th of October.

Crissixo A GHOST.—Some sensation has been caused In the neighbourhood of New Brighton, near Liverpool, by the freaks of a "ghost." Late wayfarers in the locality have been startled by the appearance of a tall figure clothed in female garments of white, whose move- ments and actions were to the nervous of an alarming character. So much uneasiness was caused that the police laid themselves out to capture the ghost, but though on several occasions they came within sight of it, the appearance of the law in its majesty appeared to have as much terror for the perturbed spirit as its own myste- rious wanderings possessed for belated individuals, and It took to its heels with such celerity as to avoid arrest The apparition, of course, was nothing more alarming than a young fellow of the district, with a turn for prac- tical joking, and it is understood that his personality is known to the police, though the latter desire to catch him in fiagraute dehcto before preferring any charge. The probability is, however, that the ghost is now "laid," for the inhabitants have begun to resent the foolish freak, and should the joker fall into their hands he is likely to be very euunsarily treated.

Sir,— It seems the Town Council are not prepared to do anything towards increasing the usefulness; of the Library until they are forced, and I hope it will not be long before they are. You have, I think, clearly proved that they are is the wrong, and this thought is strengthened by the fact that no attempt has been made to correct your ; statements. This being the case, why cannot the Council acknowledge that they have acted wrongfully, and set about inaugurating a new system by which the institution shall be absolutely free? The Library Committee must surely have some doubt as to their position, or the chairman would have answered fully the explicit question put to him at the last Council meeting respecting the authority for the course they have adopted. Is it possible the chairman did not quote his authority bec wee he cannot? For myself I fail to see why Warrington should be so far behind its neighbours in the matter of a Free Library. The present state of affairs places a young man at a great disadvantage compared with his friends in surrounding towns. My friends in St. Helens. Runcorn, and Widnes are able to go ' to their Libraries and get whatever book they require to take home, bet when I want a particular book I must go to the readine-room end attempt to study it there. This attempt, I need scarcely say, is very unsatisfactory owing to the noise of the readers crowded in the room; and I am un- fortunate in being an individual who cannot etudy in a crowd. Besides this, lam placed at a still greater disad- vantage, inasmuch as my time for frequenting the reading. roam is very limited. 1 am kept hard at work horn early morning until eight o'clock nearly every night, and ill go to Bold-street and get a book I have scarcely a chance to open it before it is time to clear out. lam sure there are ; scores similarly placed to myself who are prevented for this very teasers from availing themselves of the facilities of Institution. Why cannot we therefore have the books at the home to study at leisure ? To my mind there has been no eatisfactoryauswer yet given to that question. If the question involved the erection of a building and the purchase of all the books required as it did at Etuucorn and Widnes, our rulers might hesitate. But we in Warrington have been very favourably circumstanced in these respects. 1 The building nes long existed, and the majority of the books hive been generously given to the Library ; so that ;it only regeires the will of the authorities to make the Library a great educational factor in our town life. If our authorities had had to pick up their education as many are now trying to do, we should not now have to plead for facilities being granted to us which are enjoyed by other towns of far less • itnportance. Our Town Councillors are very fond of telling visitors of the eulightenment and pro- gress of the borough, but I, for one, would rather see the exhibition of a little enlightenment and progress rn the part of our leaders than read of any amount. Certain it is,thet those who boast so much of this enlightenment have done nothing to bring it abeut. The very mention of the agencies that would promote it—such as a Free Library and a School Board—almost sends them into fits, and they do their ut- most to prevent them being adopted. But our townspeople are gradually becoming aware of the vales of these educa- tional agencies—thanks, sir, to the columns of your paper —stud those who now oppose their wishes %%ill soon be un- able to stand before an advancing public opinion which will see that every facility for self-improvemsnt is afforded to ' those amongst us who desire to make their way Cs batter thinge.—Yours in the struggle for 1 • EQUALITY. P S little thought while I was writing tbe above that ; this subject was engaging the attention of the House of 'Commons. Yet se it was, and [ am exceedingly pleased, Mr I Editor, to find that the Attorney-General has confirmed your ; views, and most distinctly stated that the Library Commit- tee have no right to make any distinction between sub- scribers and non-subscribers. After this positive, official declaration, there will surely be no delay in making our splendid library "free" in fact as well as in name. The wonder is that such an anomalous state of things has been allowed to pass unchallenged for so long a period, and I am sure the thanks of the whole community are due to you for your exeoeure of the Consmittee's false position, and your persistent and noble efforts to convince them of the error of their ways. Personally, I congratulate you heartily upon lhe success which has so far attended your advocacy of this local fight for •• freedom, "and I trust we shall soon have the gratification of seeing the Warrington Library enter upon a career of increased usefulness.

div.head: NEED FOR A FREE LENDING LIBRARY.
div.p: THE NEED FOR A FREE LENDING LIBRARY.

Sir,—lt is highly gratifying to all friends of education that, as far as you are concerned, the right to have a Free Lending Library is not going to be allowed to die out ; and I trust the time is nigh at hand when your labour in the CAUS of trying to obtain for the people of Warrington a Free Library in reality, instead of a sham, will be accom- plished. I know that many contend that this privilege of having a Free Library we already enjoy, simply because we are free to go to the Museum and rend for ourselves the books we desire to read; or, on the other band, we can ob- tain the privilege of raking the books home by becoming subscribers for the snm of Is. 6d. per quarter. Now this may seem very plausible and satisfactory reasoning to this class of stand-still politicians; but I think that in your ar- ticle of last Saturday, dwelling on the answer of Alderman Webster to Councillor F. A Roberts' quest.ion regarding the illegality of using as a subscription library a free public library supported by the rates, ybu have proved to demon- stration that it is illegal to cltar,te a subscription at all for an institution calling itself " Free," which you might well call a mockery. _ _

Several years beck I had the pleasure of living in a town with over a quarter of a million of inhabitants that had a large Free Library, with several branches throughout the town, whereby I could take home a book to read without being compelled to be a subscriber further than paying the rate of one penny in the pound. Does it not sound to reason that in a large and populous town like that the diffi- culty of haying a Free Lending Library would be greater than in a place like Warrington? If you can vouch for the , statement you make in your article in last Saturday's "Examiner," viz • that there is not another public library in the country constituted under the Libraries' Act where a , yearly or quarterly subscription is demanded, after making a levy of one penny in the pound on the rates, then I con- tend on principle we should refuse at all hazards being com- pelled to become subscribers. With regard to the other contention that we can go to the reading room ourselves without the payment of a subscrip- tion, it only requires a little close examination to find that it is a matter of impossibility for this to be carried en any length of time with comfort to the inhabitants. I have at- tended that reading room pretty regularly for some months back, and I have been pleased beyond measure to find the room generally full in the evening, which is very satisfac- tory, considering the period of the year, when people generally prefer baying a walk, instead of being closed up in a room. I find, in looking over the minutes as pre- sented to the Council, that the visitors to the Museum during the month of July increased by 37 per cent, corn- pared with July in 18811; books issued in reading room in- creased by 27 per cant. in July compared with the same I month in 1886 ; books issued in Lending Library increased 3 per cent. I think we may fairly assume that this increase will continue, especially during the winter months. If so, there will either have to be more room provided, or else people will be compelled to remain at home, however de- sirous they may be to attend. On the other band, we may calculate that several will be compelled to stay at home during the winter season through being subject to a violent conghing, which is very unpleasant to people desiring to spend two or three hours in reading. I regret to say that I am one of those who have a passionate desire to attend the reading room; but feel that I shall have to sacrifice this desired boon for the comfort of others for the same reason I have given. And why should this be se ? Certainly, I think, we have a right to demand the privilege which the Act meant us to have, viz., a Free Lending Library.—l se- main, yours respectfully, LOVER OF EDUCATION.

Nobody was so sim- ple as to think that Alderman Webster or the Town Clerk would, upon a question being put to them, admit that in their opinion the library was being conducted in an illegal fashion. PRESCOT BDARD OF GUARDIANS. ! On Thursday afternoon the fortnightly meeting 6f the Prescot Board of Guardians was held at the Union Work- house, Whiston. There were present Mr .1 Fisher (chair- man), Rev T Chambers, Messrs James Ransen, William Middlehurst, William Swift, John Whalley, J Buckley, J W Wareing, C B Johnson, H Hulme, J Ellison, J Leetherbar- row, W Tyrer, T Eatock, J Kenwright, and S H Hartley (clerk). RELIEF.—The Workhouse Master reported there were 484 inmates of the house this week, 493 last week, and 474 in the corresponding week of last year. 'rue number ot vagrants relieved had been 85, as against 49 in the corres- ponding week last year. 111 E WORKHOUSE ALTERATIONS.— T2B Local Govern- ment Board wrote on the 12th instant acknowledging receipt of plans for carrying out certain alterations and additions to the Prescot workhouse, and intimated that the Board would cause the plans to be examined with as little delay as pos- sible. APPLICATION FOR INCREASED SALARY.-The Clerk read a corrinun cation from Mr C M Stewart, relieving officer for Windle, applying for an increase of salary. The letter stated that it was upwards of four years since his salary was last increased, and he submitted that cwing to tee Increased duties, as shown by the large increase in the amount of relief given, he might justly claim their consideration of , that application.—The letter was referred to the Finance Committee. THE ALLEGED CASE OF HYDROPHOBIA.—In accordance with the resolution pegged at the last meeting of the Board, Dr. Hall appeared before the Board in reference to the injury sustained by an inmate named Hancock,who bad been bitten by a dog at Bold.—The Chairman said some of the 0 uar- diaes were not satisfied with Dr. Hall's brief statement Diet it was a case for M. Pasteur, and they had thought they should have had further information why the man should be seat.—Dr. Hall expressed his sorrow that the Guardiane had been put to any trouble in the matter, aad said that considering the man was very badly bitten and his poor constitution he thought it was a case for M. Pasteur. There were six teeth marks—two of which did not penetrate but four did, and there were three distinct bites. tie did not at the time think there was anything more he could have told the Guardians, or he would have attended the meeting.— r, Wareing asked if the doctor would recommend a man to be ,ent to M. Pasteur before he knew whether the dog was suffering from rabies or not.—Dr Hall said that considering the constitution of the man he thought it was a case for M. Pasteur. Hydrophobia might seize the person bitten some time after baing bitten. A man was not safe for twelve months after being bitten, and he still thought in the pre- sent case there was something more than a mere dog bite.—Mr. Ranson observed that if the doctor bad given more information at the first the matter would have been all right.—The Chairman asked how the injured man , was that day.—Dr, Lien fetid he appeared to be pretty well, but there Wee certain hardness abut the wounds which he did not like. He should not like to say he was out of danger.—Mr. Wareing asked if Dr. Hall had made up his mind that M. Pasteur 'S treatment was the most effective.— Dr. Hall said he thought he was acting on the right lines.— Mr. Wareing said it had not been demonstrated that M. Pas- teur's treatment was infallible.—Dr. Hall said there was a dif- ference of opinion upon the question.—After some further discussion the Rev. T. Chambers moved that Dr. Hall's explanation be accepted as satisfactory, and Mr. J. Leatherbarrow seconded the motion, which was passed.— The Clerk afterwards asked if the Guardians had still de- cided to send the than to M. Pasteur.—After some discus- sion the Guardians considered they might safely leave the man in the bands of Dr. Hall, and not send him to Paris.— The Rev. T. Cbambers moved, and Mr. Buckley seconded, a motion to that effect, which was carried. THE COUNTY PRECEPT.—A. letter was read from Mr. T. Brawls, Town Clerk of St. Helens, dated the 14th inst., ask- ing to be favoured with a copy of the precept iseued ta the Prescot Guardians by the County Authorities last year and the year before ; and also a copy of that issued ter the current year.—The Clerk rematked that be thought the communication had reference to the charges for the police in the Prescot Division, and he had also been in correspon- dence with the Clerk of the Burnley Union on the same subject. He eugeested that he should be authorised to visit Preston and secure an interview with the Clerk of the I Peace, as the money already paid was to the end of Sep- tember, while St. Helens found its own police on the let July. The Clerk to the Burnley Union had received infor- mation that the County Authorities were under the belief that they had no authority under the law for refunding any money they might have received from poor law authorities. Certainly, if money had been paid to them to which they were not entitled, be (Mr. Hartley) thought they could be I made to refund it.—Mr. Ellison moved, and Mr. &stock seconded that the Clerk be instructed to visit Preston with the object named.—Carried. THE ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE.—On the motion ef Mr. Kenwright, seconded by Mr. Leatherbarrow' Col. F. W. Earle, J.P., was elected a member, ex-officio, of the Assess- ment and School Atteadance Coin mit es in theplace of the late Mr. H. S. Hall, J.P. THE FIRE AremieNcEs.—Mr. Wareing, in a carefully prepared lengthy report alluded to the testing of the new fire extinguishing appliances at the Workhouse, on Monday afternoon. He explained that the new steam fire engine, supplied by Messrs. Shand, Mason, and Co., the 100 feet of hose piping, fire escapes, the six cerridor tire engines, and the live fire exticteurs which they posses,ed were in first class working order, and the practical test to which they were subjected on Monday resulted very satisfactory. Tney bed also a constant water supply, and be could congratulate the Guardians upon having such effective appliances for coping with an outbreak of fire which might I occur. He only hoped they might never need Ito bring them into requisition except when re- quired for practising purposes. (Hear, hear.) Several Guardians expreesed their satisfaction with the new appliances, and cordial thanks were tendered to the St. Helens Corporation, to Mr. Gaskin, the St. ileleos water engineer, to Mr. Hale, workhouse manager, to Mr. Hartley, I clerk' and to Mr. Wareing, chairman of the Fire Precaution I Committee, for their assistance to the Guardians in obtain- ! irg the the appliances.—Mr. Wareing afterwalds novel a motion that the workhouss master be authorised to permit the use of the fire engine at any fire in the neighbourhood, I and the Rev. T. Chambers seconded the notion.—Mr. Leathetbarrow said it should be understood that when the fire engine was requited outside messengers would be ex- pected to bring their own horses to yoke to the engine.—The motion was then passed. This was the principal business.
