SEARCHING FOR "LOST MONEY" AT
ST. HELENS.

At a certain establishment in one of the main thoroughfares of St. Helens there is engaged a lively young gentleman who has recently hit upon an amusement which nightly affords him and others the utmost diversion. At a window in the upper story of a tall building this gentleman takes his position late in the evening, and commences an operation very much akin to fishing —more divert- ing, however, in its results to the "angler," though somewhat morally disastrous to the victims. Fas- tening a copper coin to the end of a reel of cotton, 1 the operator waits until a pedestrian is passing be- low, and then he drops the coin on the pavement with a merry jingle. The passer-by instantly turns, thinking he has dropped some money, and cora- -1 mences a fruitless search, to the infinite amusement lof the party at the window above. Quite recently ' a regular " masher " made a minute exploration of that particular piece of pavement, and cut a ludic- rous figure as he groped about with a couple of matches in his hands. After a time, a youth came along, and the " masher " enlisted his service with "here, my boy, I've lost half a crown;" but the united efforts of the pair failed to discover the miss- ing coin. Next, an intoxicated Irishman dropped (or rather said he had) some money on the spot, and with a continual outpouring of oaths, set up a search; but for the life of him he could not come within any spot he wanted by two yards. For son 3 hours he dodged about like a ship heaving at anchor, and was eventually joined by neighbours from across the street. Having asked what was the matter, the neighbours managed to extricate from the midst of a volley of oaths the fact that he had lost money while on his way to Earlestown. The Irish- man departed without his money, and the search was continued by the neighbours, but without. avail. Subsequently a number of boys passed ttm place, and hearing money roll on the footpath, were instantly on the look-out. A dispute, however, arose as to the ownership of the money, which all of them claimed, and they summarily proceeded to settle the point with their fists. Another evening a well-known tradesman was closing his shop when the coin dropped with a bang on the flags, and caused him to audibly ex- claim, • " There goes some money, but it can't be mine; I've none in my pockets ! " Search was made nevertheless. Out came the wife with candle and brush, and the footpath got such a sweeping_ that it does not usually receive. While engaged sweeping the coin dropped again, and one of the party re- marked, "There, I've kicked it," causing the searchers to redouble their efforts. But the party soon wearied of the work and retired. On another occasion a juvenile who got an idea of where the money rolled from, squatted on the floor until one o'clock in the morning in the vain hope of making a grab. More fortunate was an older youth, who ran his head against the suspended coin, and seizing it made off, exclaiming, "I've got it, and a lot of string with it!" That youth gave the game , away.

The annual cricket match at Widnes for the benefit of Mr. James Ihiggs,the well-known Widnes Club professiooal, took place on Saturday afternoon. The day was beautifully fine. The players included some of the most renowned on the cricket field, and as a consequence there was a capital gate, and a good game. The match was between 16 of Wid- nes and district and a Lincashire eleven captained by Mr. A. N. Hornby. Why Mr. Briggs was so highly favoured this year as regards each noted players rumour z sports as follows: 'Jack " asked 51.! Hereby if he could spare him and Watson on Saturday, as they wanted to play for lois (Briggs) father's benefit. To this nquest Mr. Hornby not only readily consented, but himself profferred to take part in the match and bring a team. This offer, it is needless to say, was as readily accepted as It was given. Unfortunately two of the players who had been announced to come (Messrs Shrewsbury and Scotton) did not put in an appearance, but very able substitutes were found. The wicket was in good condition, but the strong wind which was blowing militated slightly against bowling and fielding. The 16 went to the wickets firet, and were despatched for 67 runs, the only stand being made by "Joe" Briggs, who scored 17. On the eleven going to bat the game became more interest- ing. Mr. Hornby and Mr. E. B. Rowley faced the bow Beg of "Joe" and Briggs, senior. In a very short time a score 9f over 50 had been run up, both batsmen driving the ball in all directions. Mr. Hernby scored 16 eff one over of Joe Briggs. The Lancashire captain's innings, however, was not faultless. Moore missing him at cover point when he had scored 21. He was also missed twice by Briggs senior, once when he drove the ball straight and Briggs was bowl- ing and once at long field off. Both catches, however, were difficult ones. With the score at 74 Colqnitt relieved Briggs, senior, and soon after Joe Briggs gave way for ' Nield. The batsmen were then soon separated, Nield, in about the second over, clean bowling Hornby, whose place was taken by Mr. Jewett: The score had now reached the high figure of 86. Mr. Hornby's score of 57 included 2 six hits, 6 fours 1 three, 5 twos, and 8 eingles. Mr. Jowett was caught at cover point by Callon (ft Cal- quitt, when ha had scored six, Colquitt having missed him previously. Mr. P. Thbell followed, but made no stand, being c Reay b Nield when he had augmented • the score by four runs. Mr. R. 11. Gossage suffered a simile tate, being caught behind the wickets by White (professional, of Liverpool) di Colquitt, when he had scored eight. A stand, however, was ro.,.de when "Jack " Briggs joined Mr. Rowley. With the score at 155, and no severance effected, Joe Briggs again took the bowling off Nield. Immediately after Mr. Rowley hit his wicket. His innings, like Mr. Hornby's, was not faultless, he being missed two or three times. His score of 52 included 2 sixes, 5 fours, 6 twos, and 8 singles. When Briggs, who was joined by Mr. F. H. Goseage, jun., had made 25 he was stamped by White off Colgaitt, and his place was taken by Yates. Mr. Goaeage suffered the same fate as Briggs off Joe Briggs, when be bad scored 13, and the time for draw- ing having arrived, Yates retired, 7, not out. The score had now reached the large total of 178 for EeVen wickets, Watson, Pliling, and Mr. Bough having to bat. div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER
LONDON. THURSDAY.

Town has brightened up suddenly and strangely this week. Just at the end of the moribund session. when all interest seemed flagging, the House showed new vitality, and the life within made itself, felt without. The crowds that collected in Palace Yard consisted largely of strangers, who scrutinised the different members going in with considerable in- terest. Mr. Gladstone, fresh from his tree-felling at Hawarden, looked unusually hale, and did the weather the compliment to come out without his umbrella. I don't think I ever saw Lord Randolph look less like a Cabinet Minister or more like a patron of the turf. The Irish element was very adequately represented in the crowd, and many Roman Catholic clergy recognised their archbishop, and pointed him out to surrounding sympathisers. It is so curious to find .town beginning to fill when Parliament is beginning to disperse. But the pro- tracted session has told on many of the members, who are as keen for their holiday as schoolboys at midsummer. They have done their duty, but this last week was rather a strong order. One result of the debate, or rather of the interest in the division, has been that all the big hotels round Charing Cross have been unexpectedly full. The late session has caused many members to keep near the capital, and so Folkestone. Tunbridge Wells, Eastbourne, and places within easy access of town have been crowded. The members were ready if they -were wanted. But their houses in town have been shut up, and so, on the night of the division, or when a division was expected, they had to find sleeping quarters near the scene of their activity. The coffee room of the Grand Hotel looked more like a room in the Reform or the Carlton than a place designed for the refreshment of bona fide travellers. We have lost Mrs Langtry as a British subject, and it seems new we are going to lose her husband. We can spare him better than his wife. And the next news is that Mr. Sydney Grundy is going to bring out an original play that was intended for the London stage at an American theatre. It is to preserve his copyright, which, by the way, he will forfeit at this side of the Atlantic, that he takes this step. There are those who advocate a large measure of emigration as the cure for all the dif- ficulties of the old country, but if we are to lose our actresses and our authors we shall be in a bad way—the More so as Ambrican plays scarcely hit the English taste, and American actresses do not quite come up to our own. Foreigners are always sending over officials to see how things are done in England. And we never follow their example. The most travelled people with European boundaries, we are the slowest to take a hint or borrow a suggestion. And we seem perversely to start wrong, and then we stick to the way we began. For instance, in Germany or France you will see the postman on his way to the train emptying the different letter boxes that lie in his direction. He is saved a walk, and the public get the last possible minute for their correspondence. Our way is to take all the contents of the letter boxes back to the head office, and have them there despatched. I believe at last we shall adopt the method of France. Germany, and common sense. Latterly the French sent some of their police over here, and had them stationed at Charing Cross, Hyde Park Corner, King William-street, and other centres to watch how our constables controlled the traffic. They brought back with them practical rules,which are now enforced in Paris. In the same way the Swiss sent an officer to Victoria Station to master our method of despatching luggage with celerity. This experiment was less happy in its result, as it is said the poor man, after a week's study, gave it up and committed suicide. There has. been quite a flutter about the police raid on the Clock Tower Club, and the flutter has been the more continuous as it is understood the experiment is to be repeated in the case of two or three other gaming houses. There is the usual outcry about the high gambling in the London clubs, but the law as it now stands is perfectly clear. Where a club exists for social or political purposes, if there should be gambling, as no doubt there is at a great many of them, the police have no right to interfere. The playing may be constant and the stakes ruinous, still he law does not allow the scandal to be abated. The club is, as it were, a private house, and the police have no business on the premises. But if the club he founded and carried on for the purpose of gambling, then the law comes in and so do the police. The police well know that in the last three years the number of gambling hells has increased. It has been decided to put them down. The theatrical season began this week. We have bad novelties sind we have had revivals. It is curi- ous how Mr. Irving sets the fashion. He male Faust take by its scenery, and scenery is what managers are now bound to give their public. At the Novelty we had a play of Mr. Buchanan's, with the romantic title of the Blue Bells of Scotland. Such an " olla podrida" as it was to be sure, old matter worked up, a heartless nobleman, a lovely girl se- duced and abandoned, a cruel agent grinding the poor crofters, and that kind of frank, hearty, dar- ing young hero that Mr. H. Neville has been playing to perfection for the last twenty years. If the dramatic material was old, the scenery was brand new. A battle field at Burmah is about as recent a subject as the scene painters can represent. Miss Fortescue looked pretty, and yet America has no improved her. Henry Neville was irresistible. Miis Marie Stuart was the chief novelty, and did her little bit of Highland acting very freshly and prettily. The audience were not bored, but coma- tose, and the play achieved what is called a great success. There is just now great doubt what is going to be done with the coinage. The Jubilee issue seems to have been all absorbed. One meets the sovereigns in circulation, but very few of the shillings, and of course none of the sixpences. They already rank as curiosities, and are worth at present about half- a-crown a piece. lam told that one cause of the scarcity of the coins is that they have been largely taken up by colonists. They were issued when London was full of visitors, and there was of course an imniediate demand for them. The Americans got as many as they could. The question is, will they be re-issued? We are certainly badly off for half sovereigns, and for even half crowns. I hear it is likely the Queen's head will be re-cut, and the existing reverses retained. I am told that the crown die has been broken, and that a new one will he issued with a legend on the edge as in the George IV. crowns instead of milling. The gold .E 5 pieces sell now here at about .C 6 a piece. A good deal of this Jubilee money has been enamelled by jewellers and converted into brooches, solitaires, and sleeve links. The jewellers could be convicted for offences against the Mint, and would be subject to a very severe penalty. But it is not likely the law will be put in force. If it were, the price of these ornaments would go up enormously.

TERRIBLE RAILWAY CoLLISION NEAR DONCASTER. 21 PERSONS KILLED AND 60 INJURED. APPALLING SCENES. A terrible railway disaster occurred on Friday, at Hexthorpe siding, about a mile from Doncaster. It seems that about noon a Midland excursion train from Sheffield drew up at Hexthorpe siding for the collection of tickets, when a Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire train from Barnsley and Penistone dashed into it. The results were appalling. Car- riages were smashed by the force of the impact, and the screams of the passengers were heartrending. I Efforts were at once made to ascertain the extent of the disaster, and to succour the injured. Such of the passengers as had escaped injury or were com- paratively unhurt, leapt from both trains, but many poor creatures, dead or wofully injured, remained in the debris. Help was sum- monsed and aid telegraphed for from Doncaster I and elsewhere. The scenes disclosed by the opera- tions of the relief party, who promptly set to work, are described as heartrending. The actual number of killed is not yet forthcoming, but it is variouly i erimated at from ten to twenty-four. There s only too much reason to fear that the latter num- ber more closely approximates to fact. Many per- sons also were shockingly injured. When the news reached Doncaster, great consternation was caused. This being Cup Day Doncaster was, of course, thronged with a multitude of visitors, and some- thing like a scars has been occasioned by the Hex- thorpe disaster. Two different reports agree that about 60 persona have been injured. Officials of the Manchester, Sheffeld, and Lincolnshire Railway have proceeded to the scene of the accident by special train. Great ' excitement prevailed at Barnsley, the passengers from., that place being numerous. ADDITIONAL DETAILS. STATEMENTS BY PASSENGERS. A Sheffield correspondent telegraphs :—A terrible collision occurred in a siding one mile from Don- caster Great Northern Station. A Midland train was standing for the purpose of ticket collecting when a train from Barnsley rushed into it, causing an.awful crash. Many persons were killed. .A passenger natried,Joseph Chapman, living in Union- street, Barnsley, says he was in a carriage next the engine of the Barnsley train, which slashed into the Midland carriage. He first knew something was wrong by being thrown head foremost against a man opposite. They could tell the brake was be- ing promptly applied. On looking out of the win- dow a fearful spectacle presented itself. The engine had crushed through two carriages, and the line was strewn not only with broken carriages but with the dead and dying. The fearful cries of some sufferers were to be heard, ;while others of the victims were seen to have had their heads nearly knocked off and their bodies horribly mutilated. Nearly, if not all, the dead and wounded are Sheffielders. "Tremendous excitement has been caused throughout the town, and thousands are rushing off to the scene of the calamity. The news spread like wildfire, the collision being said to be the most fearful that has happened in the district for years. The telegraph office was thronged with persons who have escaped desirons of communi- cating with their friends. The railway officials are rendering all possible aid in extricating the dead and wounded, and willing helpers are volunteering their services. Mr. William Beattie, of Fieldhead-road, Sheffield, says: lam much knocked about, as I was in a composite carriage when the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire engine ran into it. It contained eight apartments in addition to the guard's van. The carriage was completely telescoped. The guard, whose name is Chandler, of Sheffield, was, fortuna- tely, out of the van at the time. The collision was awful as the result shows only too vividly. Up to the sixth compartment, the train was altogether telescoped. Timber was flying right and left, with mangled corpses and many injured, all over the line. I should think quite twenty persons are dead.. The engine came at full speed, and, in my opinion, the flag signals could not have been regarded. Mr. Verity, the waggon-builder of Mexborough, is among the injured. I am told that dismembered bodies have been dragged out of the debris, and that amongst the ruins were many arms and legs. The Press Association correspondent telegraphing at 2-15 says: Some persons were cruShed so badly that they could not be extricated until portions of the carriages were removed, and a still larger num- j3er were injured severely. From fifty to sixty per- sons have already been conveyed to Doncaster Infirmary. The Penistone train was the express from Liverpool to Hull. Up to five o'clock on Friday afternoon 23 corpses had been recovered from the ruins of the Midland special train, and between 50 and 60 injured. Most of the injured were taken to Doncaster Infirmary, where a few have since died. An unusual propor- tion of the injuries were of a serious character, and many of a shocking description. One headless corpse was found.

div.head: MR. BRUNNER, M P., AND THE IRISH
div.p: MR. BRUNNER, M P., AND THE IRISH

CAUSE. SPEECH AT CORK. There was a great meeting, on Saturday even- ing, at Cork, which was addressed by Mr. Labou- chere, Mr. Brunner, and Mr. Ellis. We take the fol- lowing report of Mr. Brunner's speech from the "Cork Examiner' : Mr. Brunner, M.P. for Northwich. who was re- ceived with great warmth, said—Ladies and gentle- men, I am very much afraid, and rather sorry for you on that account, that after listening to Mr. Labouchere a speech from me will be like taking a glass of very flat ale after a bumper of champagne. My heart has gone out to you while Mr. Labouchere has been talking to you. I am, as my friend Mr. Hooper has described, the latest messenger to you from the British democracy—(cheers)—and I want to assure you that you have now nothimrto do but to wait and victory is in your hands. Of this I am perfectly convinced, that the five thousand men who voted for me four weeks, ago to-day are representative of the millions of men in the north of England who are ready to do justice to Ireland—(cheers)--and that the time is come when you may cease to hate , the Government of Dublin Castle, and afford to treat it with contempt. (Cheers.) The story that we have to tell of what happened yesterday is a sad one; and I trust in God that the tact that such a scene as that has been witnessed for the first time by Eng- lish members of Parliament will make it very nearly the last that will happen. (Cheers.) My friend. Mr. Labouchere, a few weeks ago asked me whether I would accompany him to witness Wil- liam O'Brien's trial, and I consented. Well, he is not tried yet—(cheers)—but when he is tried I mean to be there, and I mean to tell the people that I love William O'Brien as they do, and I mean to bid them follow in • his foot- steps. (Cheers.) I mean to bid them hold by the rights that are as common—or ought to be—to you as the people who live in Great Britain. I mean to tell them to stand fast by their homes— (loud cheers)—and I mean to tell them to stand fast by the league that is proclaimed as a dangerous and wicked association. (Cheers.) Oh, yes ! I will qualify for six months. (Laughter and cheers.) I came over to tell the Irish people that there is no need for outrage—that the best they can do for thenfselves and for us in Great Britain is to con- tinue calm and peaceabfe, as they have been for months past. (Hear, hear.) There is no need for outrage, and depend upon it you have but to be still and hold firm to- gether, for your friends, who are rapidly growing in number in Great Britain will do your work for you. (Cheers.) Why is it that the story which we English members, will tell the House of Commons in a few days is likely to bring that brutal system of constabulary rule to an end? lam sorry to say that it is for the reason that a very large number of my fellow-countrymen have been influ- enced by the hideous slanders uttered against you. I believe, and I am sorry to say y, that the words coming from us will have more influence upon the English people than the words that have come in denial of those slanders from your representa- tives in the Imperial House of Commons. I promise you that so far as my strength will avail that story will be told wherever I can find hearers throughout England. (Cheers.) And I want to tell you now,. as I mean to tell my fellow-members in the House of Commons on Monday night, that the varying accounts which appeared in the London papers and in the Irish Tory papers are utterly false and lying acc3unts of the affair that happened at Mitchels- town. I declare to you, having seen the whols of the proceedings with my own eyes yesterday after- noon, that the break-up of the meeting was the result of the utterly wanton and unprovoked attack of the police upon the people—(hear, hear, and cheers)—and that the firing from the police barrack was not at all in defence of the safety of the police,

but an utterly brutal attempt to kill men who I could do them no harm. There were only a few shots fired, and as I heard that there were five men who received gunshot wounds, it looks uncom- monly like aiming at individuals (hear, hear,) and I shall not be satisfied unless there is a fair and impartial investigation into what was done yesterday by the police. (Cheers.) Mr. Labouchere has told you some- thing of what the "Times" says of him. Well, it has also something to say of me. 1 don't say that the other, the "Irish Times"—is much better. (Hear, hear.) I abould begin to feel ashamed of myself if either of them began to praise me, One of the Irish Tory papers says that a thousand men were playing at football with three policemen'shelmets. (Laughter.) Well, to give you accurate• informa- tion the fact is that. five men played football with one helmet, and that is magnified into a thousand men playing with three helmets. I have gone , through a fight lately, and like many other English members have to thank the Iribh members for the Very effective help they gave me. (Cheers.) I consider ikis only like give twelve pence for a shil- ling, if I come and help the Irish members in Ire- land. (Cheers.) lam here readyto do it, but there are precious faveof your representatives who want help: However. it may be that I am not helping one iudividual,but the whole eighty-six 11Np:there. (Cheers.) If you will take what I have said to you here to-night in that spirit I shall be heartily grate- ful to you and love you all the more. (Cheers.) MIL BRUNNER AND THE NATIONAL LEAGUE. The following is the full text of the letter from Mr. Brunner, M.P., which was read at the meeting of the National League in Dublin on Tuesday : Winnington Old Halt, Northwich, 3rd Sept., 1887. Dear Mr. Harrington.—l desire to become a mem- ber of the National League of Ireland. You will no doubt understand clearly that I do not men to imply apprlval in detail of all the objects of the League. With its main object, however—the pro- motion of the happiness, the freedom, and the pros- perity of the people of Ireland—l am in heartiest sympathy. My desire is simply to offer a strong protest against the policy of the Tory Government and of their supporters in the House of Commons. It is a wicked policy, for the reason that it tempts the Irish people to adopt again the old and bad method of secret meeting in anger and despair, in- I stead of the method, still almost new to Ireland, of' acting together in the open light of day in peace and seburitv. It is no less a contemptible and a ridiculous policy because it is foredoomed to failure. It failee in strong hands, the hands of Spencer and Forster; it will fail signally in the very different hands of Londonderry and Balfour. It failed when backed by an almost unanimous people in Great Britain, It will fail again now that it is condemned by a large and a powerful party, supported, as I , believe it to be, by the vast majority of the people of this country, and its failure will speedily bring upon its authors overwhelming confusion and con- tempt.-1 am, dear sir, yours faithfully, JOHN T. BRUNNER.

T. Harrington, Esq., M.P., Secretary. GIFT OF ONE THOUSAND POUNDS. The "Daily News" of Friday says :—A cheque for -a thousand pounds accompanied the letter from Mr. Benner, M.P., which we publish this morning. It is his handsome practical testimony of sympathy with the Irish people. Mr. Brunner has seen for himself the nature of the distress in Ireland. has thought of a schemb for its temporary alleviat tion. He places his plans before our readers; and, acting on the good principle that practice is better than precept, gives his money at the same time as his advice. He is too sincere a friend of the Home Rule cause not to be desirous to allay "the bitter strife, almost amsuntinp,, to civil war, and the exasperation which leads to outrage and moonlighting." This happy result, however, he , thinks can only be abhieyed by some plan, as he suggests, for enabling the poor in Ireland "to tide over the gathering difficulties of their lot during the coming winter months, and to foster the gro rang love between the peoples of the two islands and the nascent hope of better and brighter days to come." His munificent donation is therefore given to start an Irish People's Relief Fund. He proposes that acute cases of distress shall be relieved, that legal and other necessary aid shall be offered to tenants in danger of eviction, and that steps shall be taken to "replace the kindly and moderating in- fluence of Sir Medvers Buller." No names more likely to command public confidence than those of. Lord Spencer, Lord Aberdeen, and Lord Wolverton could have been given as trustees of this happily devised fund. Dr. Tuke's assistance in the matter of relief works will be invaluable, and the idea of entrusting the collection and disbursement of the fund to a commission representing England, Scot- land, Wales, and Ireland emphasises the conviction of the Liberal Home Rulers that it -is their policy which conduces to true union.

div.p: THE FXAMINTM S TTRD Y. SEPTEMBER 17. 1887.

giving the Royal Assent to various bills passed by both Houses, and also for the prorogation of Parliament. The Speaker, preceded by the Sergeant-at-Arms carrying the mace, and attended by most of the members present, then proceeded to the House of Peers. The Speaker returned, attended by the Strgeant-at•Arms, but minus the mace, and, taking his position near the chair, took leave of th, members present, who passed kefore him in single file, each member shaking hands with the right bon, gentleman as he left the House. Thus ended the memorable session of 1887.

PROROGATION OF PARLIAMENT. THE QUEEN'S • SPEC. The House of Lords met at a quarter to twelve, when the Royal assent was given by commission to the Appropriation and several other Acts. The Queen's Spevch was read as follows by the Lord Chancellor, the Sneaker and members of the House of Com- mons attendinz at the Bar of the House :

MY LORDS AND GENTLEMEN, My relations with other Powers continue to be friendly. The protracted negotiations which have taken place be- tween the Emperor of Russia and myself in regard to the line of frontier which we should agree to recognise as form- ing the northern limit of Afghanistan have been brought to a satisfactory termination, and the Ameer has readily accep- ted the boundary which the Powers have laid down. I hope that this Convention will conduce ppwerfully to the main- tenance of a durable peace in Central Asia. The treaty between Great Britain and China in reference to the relations of that country with Burmah has been rati- fied. The confident hope which I expressed. that the general pacification of the latter country would be effected during thrspresent year, has been fully realised, and a set- tled Government is being gradually introduced into its more remote districts. A Convention was concluded between the Sultan of Turkey and myself for the parpose of defining the conditions under which it would be possible for me to undertake the with- drawal of my troops from Egypt at a fixed date. It has, however, not been ratified by the Sultan, and the course of action imposed upon me by my obligations to the ruler and people of Egypt remains unchanged. The presence of my forces has secured to that country the blessings of tran- quility, and has enabled me effectually to support the Khe- dive in his efforts to promote the good government and prosperity of his people. I have agreed with the President of the United States to refer to a joint Commission the difficult questions respecting the North American Fisheries, which have recently been under discussion between the two nations. It is with singu- lar satisfaction that I mention the assemblage of the first Conference of the representatives of my colonies that has ever been held in this capital. Their deliberations, directed to many matters of deep practical interest to their respective Communities, and conducted in a spirit of hearty co-opera- tion, will, I doubt not, add strength to the aff,ction by which the various parts of my Empire are bound together. GENTLEMEN OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS. I thank you for the liberal roovision which you have made for the wants of public service.

Mr LORDS AND GENTLEMEN There are some grounds for hoping that the grave de- pression under which all commercial and industrial interests In this country have lain for so long is assuming a less severe character. I deeply grieve to add, however, that there is no mitigation of the suffering under which large portions of the agricultural cemmunity continue to labour. The wants and difficulties of Ireland have occupied your close attention during a protracted session. I trnst that the remedies which your wisdom has provided will gradu- ally effect the complete restoration of order in that coun- try, and will give a renewed encouragement to peaceful in- dustry. In order to pass them it has been necessary to postpone the consideration of many important measures affecting other parts of the United Kingdom, which I , doubt not you will be able to resume without hind- rance in the coming session. I have, however, gladly given my assent to legislation by which I hope the provi- sion of allotments in districts where they are required will be facilitated. The safety and prosperity of the large l and industrious population engaged in mining operations will be more fully secured, and hal:ill:tient practices in the marking of mer- chandise highly injurious to the trade, and the commercial relation of this country, will be prevented, while, with re- gard to Scotland, the law of criminal procedure will be simplified and improved, and the high office of Secre- tary for Scotland will acquire additional importance and efficiency. This year, as the fiftieth anniversary of my reign, has been the occasion of a fervent loyalty on the part of my subjects throughout the empire which has deeply touched me lam indeed truly grateful for the warm and hearty proofs of affection which have reachd me from all classes. And in thanking God for the blessings he has vouchsafed to me and to my country, I trust I may be spared to continue to reign over a lovinr, faithful, and united people. HOUSE OF COMMONS. FRIDAY AFTERNOON. The Speaker took the chair at 1-45, at which hour there was but a limited attendance ef members. The SPEAKER announced the receipt of a letter from Mr. Eaton. resident magistrate, Cork, intimating that Win. O'Brien, had been committed to Cork prison to take his trial on a charge under the Criminal Law Procedure (Ireland) Act, on September 23. Shortly after two o'clock the Usher of the Black Rod advanced to the table and summoned the House to the \ Roue of Peers t, Her Majesty's Royal COMMiagOR for

div.head: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER. LFROM OUR OWN CORRESPONDENT.] 23, Old Broad-strent, E.C.
div.p: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER. LFROM OUR OWN CORRESPONDENT.] 23, Old Broad-strent, E.C.

The directors of the Bank of England 'nada no change in the rate of discount on Thursday, which consequenely re mains at 4 per cent. This is sufficient evidence that the fear of immediate heavy withdrawals of gold are grounri- less, and the critics of the ae‘ioa or want Of action of the Bank of England directors in not raising the rate to 5 per cent., are once again shown t be far less able to guage the floancjal position than the men they would instruct. The Stock Exchange has been almost solely occupied with the fortoightly settlement,which is by no mesas a heavy one. Thelear of dearer money engendered by many writers has its effect on carrying over rates. but the charges were not so onerous as they promised to be. Home Rails still continue dull, due rather by the abeence of support than from unfavourable traffic returns. Foreign Stocks are perhaps the dullest markets, the un- certainty of the future, the fear of the unknown,acd genera suspicion, causing market lifelessness in these stockstand in- vestors should fight shy of them altogether. On the other hand American securities although not so strong as they were, still show buoyancy, and with the re- mov rl of the apprehensions of dear money the market would go up with a bound. The statement by the Government that they are unable to introduce the Bill to Amend the Companies Acts this cession was tally expected, but the crying evil of the pre- sent state of affairs has become so pronounced that the Government will have to make it one of the first subjects for next session. This delay is to be regretted as it gives six months license for some of the most reckless and un- scrupulous promoters to launch their schemes without fear of breaking the law, The last few days have seen the departure from the city of a notorious company promoter. and a well known out- side broker. The latter gained a reputation for flooding the country with its monthly circulars of advice, which were to invest in those he had shares of. In both cues there Lave been urgent inquiries as to the whereabouts of the gentle- men, but wi`hout any result. Country investors especially will be released from the temptations which these unscru- puloos but clever people knew only too well how to place In their paths, the chief, it must be admitted, being the bait of IA dividends.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS,
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS,

The fortnightly meeting of this Board WAS held at the Workhouse, Dutten. on Tuesday. Col. Ashton presided, and there were present the Revs. J. Lockwood, T Whitley, wad J W. N. Tanner ; Messrs. T. Hewitt, J. Warburton, J. Mcln- tyre, E. Aaron, J. W. Kirkham, W. Turner, E. Wallington, J. Smith, J. Brandreth, T. Lewis, T. Hadfield, J. Davies, J. Stokes, J. Campkin, Henry Percival,William Fisher, S Tay- lor, H. J. Grice, and G. Kirkham, with the clerk (Mr. H. Linaker) and deputy clerk (Mr. W. H. Linaker). THE WEAVER TRUST. A letter was read from the general manager of the Weaver Trust, informing the Board that the trustees bad paid £15,000 per annum to tbe county for the last four Years, and that the Runcorn and Northwich Boards of Guar- dians had not only got the benefit of those sums in the re- duction of their county rates, but had received about £3,000 per annum fro= the trustees for poor rates paid to the town- chips through which the river Weaver passed.—The Clerk Bela he had written a reply to that letter to the effect that he had stated to the Board that the trus- tees had paid £15,000 per annum to the county, and not £5,000 in some years, and nothing in others.— Toe Deputy Clerk reported that in reply to the letters sent out to 49 local bodies in the county, some had replied that they would not move in the matter with reference to the Weaver Trust at preeent; one, Warrington, considered they had no locus standi ; another deferred the considera- tion of the matter for some time ; others asked for further information before they took any action, and two local bodies had written to the effect that they were prepared to take action.—Mr. Hadfield : Out of 49 inquiries you have only received two replies to the effect that the authorities are prepared te take action.—The Deputy ederk : Until they get further information.—Mr. Hadfield said it seemed, to him that if the question was to be gone into properly, they must have the whole of the Cheshire Boards behind I their back. For they themselves to try to upset a corpora- tin which had been established for a large number of years and which had been confirmed by Act of Parliament, would be simple foolishness.—Me Aaron argued that if the Weaver Trust were managed by a body selected by the ratepayers, or managed the same as the Bridgewater Navigation they should not have a penny county rate to pay. There, how- ever, they had earls, dukes, and lords who knew very little about the trust. He proposed the formation of a small committee.—Mr. Grice thought it would be wise to form a small committee, according to Mr. Aaron's suggestion, and he seconded the proposal. It was evident that there was a great revenue derived from the Weaver Trust, and the sur- plus derived from it ever the expenditure belonged to the ratepayers of the county. The profits that arose from it depended upon its management, and he was of opinion that if a body of men were elected by the ratepayers of the county at different times for three years those men would look after the interests of the county. There was no fault to be found with the present trustees individually, and no oae desired to say an improper word about them. As the agitation had been commenced he thought a small com- mittee should be appointed to confer with the different , authorities, to give Veem the necessary information, and to state the basis of their action in the .natter, and also to show the necessity for having the electien of representa- tives on that trust in the hands of the ratepayers. He, therefore, seconded Mr. Aaron's motion.—Mr. Fisher moved an amendment that no conernittee be formed. If the mover and seconder of the motion that day hid any direct charge that they could bring against the present trustees of the river Weaver Trust, he should like them to bring it ; but he had not heard anything vet against them. He asked why a change was desired. Surely the gentlemen of that Beard did not doubt for oats moment the honesty of the trustees; but if there was any mismanagement, he should say let them call their attention to it, and if the trustees did not alter it, let them then take action. It would be a serious matter for the county to take action against them now.—Mr. Aeneer : I did not say that they were dishonest, I said they don't know anything, or care anything.—Mr. HADFIELD seconded Mr. Fisher's amendment, and remarked that the trust had been in existence for a large number of years. and the trustees had made it what it was. It seemed to hint that it would be rather mean to go behind their becks, and take from them the power they had as the River Weaver Navigation Company. They had, es had been admitted. no fault to find with the trustees, and if they went to Parliament he asked what would the expense be. They could not so to Parliament for the smallest thing for less thaa about £l,OOO, and if they went in respect to this matter it would cool the county thousands of pounds.— Mr. Fisher was ot opinion that the Board stood that day in a worse position than they did a fortnight age.—The Clerk said if he were a trustee of the River Weaver Trust he would wish for an enquiry like the one which was sought in order to set the matter at rest. There was a great deal of misanprehenseon existing in the county, and in their own interest it would be a good thing for the trus- tees to have an inquiry and thus set the matter at rest.— For the motion ten voted, and eight against, and the Chair- man declared the former to be carried. THE RELIEF SUPERVISION COMMITTEE.

The report of this committee was read, and reference was made to the action which was being taken with regard to the collection of money due to the Guardians—Mr. Fisher moved the adoption of the report. Mr. Hadfield said that several hundreds of pounds were outstanding. It would be more difficult to get it in the longer the subject was left over. Was nothing being done in the matter, and were the Board to keep going on, month after month, in the manner they were, without having some settlement with their collector ?—The Rev J. Lockwood said it was a matter of great importance to the Board, and it was advisable to go gently about that work, which was not standing still. A fortnight ago the clerk was instructed to apply for payment in several specified cases, and this had been done, with the result that money had been recovered in some instances. It was only fair to the collector to say that he had informed Mr Fisher that he had not received any notification on the previous morning of that meeting. The Clerk said that since the committee commenced the in• vestigation about £7O had been paid in to the treasurer.—Mr Fisher remarked that Mr 'Hadfield would find that the clerk had full instructions to deal with every case where money was outstanding. Of course, every cage had not been dealt with up to the present —Mr Hadfield said he was not speaking exactly about the committee; but thought the collector should not be left in his present position, nor the Board in its present state with reference to the matter—The report was adopted.
UNPAID CALLS. Mr. Hadfield proposed, and Mr. Aaron seconded, that proceedings be taken against the townships which had not p lid the calls made upon them.—The proposition was carried.

SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. The report of this committee was read, from which it ap- peared that the estimated amount req iireo for the expenses up to the 20th December was £ll ss.—The report was adopted. The rest of the business was routine.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. A monthly meeting of this body was held on Tuesday afternoon, at the Widnes Town Hall. Mr. F. H. Gossage presided, and there were also present Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. J. Houghton, S. Sadler, J. Taylor, F. Heyes, R. Cook, J. Midwood, D. Wright, W. W. Gossage, J. Handley, E. Carey, J. T. Allen (clerk), I. Carr (gas and water en- gineer), W. Cooper (medical officer of health), and J. Dick- son (nuisance inspector).

div.head: NETHERLRY BROOK.
div.p: NETHERLRY BROOK.

The Clerk said that in accoidanca with the instructions of the Board be bad atteuded a Local Government Board inquiry at the office of the Havton Local Board. The state of Netherley Brook was pointed out to the Inspectsr of the Local Government Board, and he (the clerk) understood that the Local Government Board had refused to sanction the loan asked for until some provision is made to keep the brook in a satisfactory state. THE LIVERPOOL WATERWORKS, &C., ACTS. The Clerk said that he bad received a copy of the Liver- pool Waterworks and Improvements Act of 1887, which contained that Board's agreements and clauses in respect of water supply.

peered down it to such an extent that on one day it was about ten inches deep. They thought that it was cnly necessary to point out the defect to have it remedied. They were told that a grid that bad been put down was totally inadequate for anything like heavy rains.—Mr. Carey said that on a previous occasion the surveyor was instructed to put on a man to keep the gullies thoroughly cleaned out, and it was hoped that that would be sufficient until certain roads were completed. It seemed, however, that that was not the case, and the inspector thought it would be better to put In some larger gullies to take away the flow of water.— The matter was referred to the Highway Committe to be dealt with.—Mr. Rossiter, 22, Lugsdale-road, wrote to the Board complaining of annoyance caused through clay being placed on the footpath and in front of his shop door during the work in connection with the new sewer. He complained that his customers could not get to his house, and that in consequence he had suffered great loss.—Mr. Carey said 1 that the material complained of would be removed as soon as possible. The contractor was responsible frir the iecon- venience.—Dr. O'Keeffe said that the contractor must not be accommodated to the injury of the occupiers of houses, who were either directly or indirectly ratepayers. In this case a small shopkeeper had suffered considerable damage, and the Board, as the guardians of the public, would be simply neglecting their duty unless they protected the rate- payers, the poor as well as the rich. He knew of a lady who lived in the neighbourhood who had to climb over a wall to get to church last Sunday. He hoped that the committee would recommend that compensation be paid to the persons who had suTered loas.—Mr. Carey said that he had particularly cautioned the contractor against stopping footpaths; why he had done so in this case he (Mr. Carey) did not know.—Mr. Sadler described the state of things as disgraceful —The Chairman: It seems to be a case in which the contractor is entirely responsible, and I think the cotn- mittee ahotrid consider the matter, and tecommend what they think is right.—lt was finally resolved that the sur- veyor be instructed to have the matter complained of removed within twenty-four hours,

div.head: SEWERAGE SCITEMB.
div.p: THE SEWERAGE SCITEMB.

The Local Government Board wrote that they had under consideration the report made by their inspector, Major Tulloch, after the inquiry held by him with reference to the application of the Widnes Local Board for sanction to bor- row £lO,OOO for works of sewage. The Board understood from Major Tulloch that the proposed works include the construction of a new outfall sewer discharging into the river Mersey below high-water mark, and they wished to inquire whether the consent a the Board of Trade had been obtained to such of the works as would be below high-water mark. The Board also observed that the Local Board had only raised £23,840 under the sanction granted them in September, 1880, to borrow £38,800 for works of sewerage. It was requested that the Board might be furnished with an explanation of the difference between the estimated and the actual expenditure on the works, all of which are stated to have been carried out. It was also desired that the sanction to the loan of £38,800 might be returned to the Board, in order that it might be cancelled, except so far as it had been called upon.—The matter was left in the hands of the clerk.
THE AUDIT. The Clerk reported that the audit had been fixed for Monday next.
ENQUIRIES.

A Mr. Millar, writing to the Clerk from Ilnyton, said : " I invite you on behalf of our Associatios, convened to gain accurate intelligence respecting the rateable amount of property registered for annual taxation in each township around this section of Lancashire, and also the salary paid to the law clerk retained by each Local Board."—The Chair- man : As to the salary of the law clerk I do not think we have such an expensive animal. (Laughter.) I think the answer should be that we have not a law clerk. The gen- tleman does not explain to what Association he belongs.
COMPLAINTS FROM RATEPAYERS.

The Clerk -re-ad a letter from Messrs. R. and Co., Warrington, saying that they were instructed by Messrs. John Fairclough and Sons to Write to the Board on the sub- ject of their warehouse at the bottom of John-street. The street, it seemed, was insufficiently bewared, and the water

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

Yesterday the races for the Doncaster Cup was tun with the following result :—Carlton lo Pythagoras 2, Royal Rose 3. Three ran. At the Iron and Steel Institute at Manchester, on Friaay, a discussion took place on the basic open-hearth process, which was advocated as giving greater strength to metal and economizing fuel. Pleasant intelligence has been received at Pembroke that the Admiralty have given orders at their dockyard for the building et two gunboats, some forty-five tons larger than those at present on the stocks in the yard. Mr, W. J. Evelyn, M.P., Conservative, writes to his Dept- ford constituents that he thinks the police exceeded their duty at Mitchelstown ; and, rather than sanction any violent and cruel proceedings against the Irish, he would vacate his seat.

THE MITCHELSTOWN RIOT.—The inquest was resumed on Friday, when Dr. O'Neill gave the results of his post-mortem examination of the three deceased men. In the cases of Shinnick and Casey buckshot bad entered the brain, and there broken in two. On Friday afternoon the Barnsley magistrates committed William Roberts. of Walsall, to one month's imprisonment in default of paying £2 and costs, for personating a police officer and obtaining admission to the house of Mrs. Wal- kinson, farmer, Worsbro'. A CRIMEAN RELIC —There has just died at Kendal an old pensioner named William Lindsay, from whose neck has been extracted a bullet which the deceased receive durinc the Crimean war. The bullet is the size of a marble, and had been in deceased's neck for 33 years. It was removed by a doctor shortly after Lindsay's death. BOLTON STRIKE.—The balance in favour of the strike fund now amounts to about £l,lOO. The expenditure for the week was £5OO, and the receipts £440, of which £320 came from districts outside Bolton. It is feared there will be a split on the arbitration proposals in consequence of
the masters declining to discharge imported men to make room for their old hands.
A REVOLT IN INDIA.

Intelligenca has been received in Bombay that an unarmcessful revolt has occurred in Millipore. The rebels suc- ceeded in penetrating into the Maharajah's Pslace, but were ultimately repulsed, nine of their number being killed and many wounded.

div.head: HIGHWAY COMMITTEE.
div.p: HIGHWAY COMMITTEE.

This committee met on the let instant, and passed various recommendations. Accou its amounting to £lB7 3s 8d were passed for payment, and the estimate of wages for the next four weeks was stated to amount to £36 per week. It was reported that the contractor had completed the main line of sewer in Victoria-roach, from Witt-road to Oilier-street, and be was now engaged in sewering in Lugsdale-rood. The Rail- way Company had completed the curbing and metalling of the road at the Warrington-road end, and the Board's work- men were engaged lifting the present road to meet the levels of the new road. The western approach to the bridge had been rolled. It was. also recommended that P. Hill's tender to supply cart for £2O be accepted ; that the usual notices, under the Public Health Act. 1875,, eec. 150, be served upon the property owners, to pave, &a., that portion of Ditton-road from Messrs. Todd Bros. works to Victoria- road; and that instructions be given to Gas Committee to lay new gas main in Lugsdale new road. T. R. Wylde wrote to the committee claiming £5 for personal injuries, dm., received in falling into Victoria-road sewer, and in- structions were given to deny liability.—The minutes of the committee were approved, on the motion of Mr. Carey, seconded by Mr. Houghton.

div.head: GENERAL& puirxons COMMITTEE.
div.p: GENERAL& puirxons COMMITTEE.

The report submitted by this committee was a short one. It recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £332 49 2d. The minues were agreed to on the proposition of Mr Carey, seconded by Mr Wright.

div.head: GAS, AND. WATER.: COMMITTEE.
div.p: GAS, AND. WATER.: COMMITTEE.

The report of this committed was adopted without dis- Cession On the motion of Mr. Wright, seconded by Mr. Sad- ler. In contained the usual report with regard to Stocks Well, and stated that ties mean rainfall for the past month had been 152 inches. The water in stock on A uvust 24th was 10.7 6,030 gallons. The illuminating power of the gas during the mynth had avoraged 17 31 candles. The sum rtquired for wages during the next four weeks for gas and water works was Y.,35- per week, and the month's accounts amounted to £5Ol 13s 4d, for gas works, and £133 IN 9d for water works.
MEDICA.L ouncv.h7s REPORT.

. The report of toe Metheil Officer stated that for August the births bad numbered 100, bein4 at the rate of 400, per 1,000, and the deaths had reached 94, being at the rate of 376 per 1,000. There bad been 36 deaths of children under one year, and 27 of children between one and five pears old. Zymotic diseases had been responsible for 31 deaths and five impests had been held. At the Accident Iluspital there were at the time of the last meeting 4 patients, and 3 had been admitted since. Five had been discharged, leaving two remaining. lathe Inspector's report for August it was stated that there had been 20 fatal Cases of diarrhosi, 8 of dysentery, and one each of scarlet fever, enteric fever and measles.

div.head: FOOD, INSPECTION.
div.p: FOOD, INSPECTION.

It was reported that the usual food inspection had been made during last month, and the following food had been de- stroyed :-23 lbs. of beef, 14 lbs. of fish, 17 lbs. apples, 10 lbs. onions, and 5 qts. plums

div.head: MARKET.
div.p: THE MARKET.
The receipts for the month were reported as being L=is 7d, being an increase of £3 83 Id as compared with August of last year.
FINANCE COMMITTEE.

The members of this Committee met on the 7th inst. and transacted financial business, afterwards recommending that a number of accounts be paid. The report that they sub- mitted to the Board was adopted without db,cussien, on the motion of Mr. Handley, seconded by Mr. Wright. This was all the business of public interest.

ANNIVERSARY SERMONS.—Anniversary sermons in con- nection with Ly'mm Primitive Methodist Chapel were preached in the chapel, in Eagle-brow, on Sunday. The preacher, both in the afternoon and evening, was the Rev. W. Evans, who has recently been appointed to Lymrrt in place of the Rev. J W. Kirkland. In the afternoon the rev. gentleman took for his subject the feeding of,the 5,000, aud in the evening he delivered a very impressive discourse on the trials of Job. Collections were made at each service on behalf of the trust turd, and a very satisfactory amount was realised. Owing to the unsettled weather many peo- ple from a distance were prevented from attending.
